The name is `prefix`, a dash and a random suffix, so callers using the same prefix each get their own directory. Nothing removes it for you; call `deleteAll` when you are done.

entries.name: IO
entries.summary:
Console input and output.

`IO` is a capability: its functions act on the outside world, so only `foul` code and `main` can call them. The exception is `inspect`, which writes a debugging view of a value and returns the value, so it can go in the middle of a chain.

```kex
main do
  IO.print("name? ")
  let name = IO.getLine.or("world")
  IO.printLine("hello, ${name.trim}")
end
```

entries.name: printLine
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stdout followed by a newline.

Any `Showable` value prints through its `show`, so numbers, lists, maps and records need no conversion. With no argument it prints an empty line.

entries.name: print
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stdout without a newline.

Use it to build a line from several pieces, or to print a prompt that the answer is typed next to.

entries.name: inspect
entries.summary:
Writes a colored rendering of `val` and its type to stderr, and returns `val` unchanged.

Since it returns its argument, `inspect` can be put in the middle of a chain to see what passes through, and taken out again later. It writes to stderr, so a program's piped stdout stays clean. The type checker treats it as pure, so pure functions can call it too.

To get the rendering as a `String`, use `inspected`.

entries.name: getLine
entries.summary:
Reads one line from stdin, without its line ending.

Returns `None` at the end of the input and also when the read fails, which is usually what interactive code wants. Use `IO.readLine` to tell the two apart. Same as `IO.in.getLine`.

entries.name: readLine
entries.summary:
Reads one line from stdin, without its line ending, and reports a failed read as an error.

Returns `Ok(None)` at the end of the input, and an `Error` only when the input cannot be read as text. Same as `IO.in.readLine`.

entries.name: getChar
entries.summary:
Reads one character from stdin, as a one-character `String`.

Same as `IO.in.getChar`.

entries.name: printError
entries.summary:
Writes `msg` to stderr followed by a newline.

Diagnostics go to stderr so that the program's output on stdout can be piped or redirected on its own. It only prints; the program keeps running.

entries.name: out
entries.summary:
Standard output, as a handle.

`IO.printLine(x)` and `IO.out.printLine(x)` both write to stdout. The handle is for passing to a function that takes a `Writable`, so the caller chooses where it writes. `IO.error` and `IO.in` are the other two standard streams.

The handle types say what each stream allows: writing to `IO.in` or reading from `IO.out` is a compile error, as it is for a file opened `Read`.

Getting a handle is pure; reading or writing through it is `foul`. `Mock.IO` captures writes made through `IO.out` as well as through `IO.printLine`, but a `with IO = ...` override replaces only calls to the `IO` functions.

entries.name: error
entries.summary: Standard error, as a handle: where `IO.printError` writes.

entries.name: in
entries.summary: Standard input, as a handle: where `IO.getLine`, `IO.readLine` and `IO.getChar` read from.

entries.name: JSON
signatures: parse(text: String, options: {Atom: Bool}) -> Result<Any, JSONError>

entries.name: JSONError
entries.summary:
Why a document could not be parsed. Every variant except `UnknownOption` carries the character position where the parser stopped.

```kex
JSON.parse("[1, 2")    # => Error(UnexpectedEnd(5))
JSON.parse("// c\n1")  # => Error(UnexpectedCharacter("/", 0))
```

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(text: String, options: {Atom: Bool}) -> Result<Any, JSONError>
entries.summary:
Parses a strict JSON document.

The text must be one JSON value; anything after it is a `TrailingInput` error. Objects come back as maps with string keys, arrays as lists, and `null` as `None`.

entries.name: fields
entries.summary:
Returns the fields of a parsed object, or `{}` for any other value.

`parse` returns `Any`; use this to read it as an object.

entries.name: items
entries.summary: Returns the elements of a parsed array, or `[]` for any other value.

entries.name: stringify
entries.summary:
Renders a Kex value as strict JSON text.

Maps become objects, lists arrays, `None` `null`, and strings are escaped. Atom keys become strings, so `{ name: "Ada" }` becomes `{"name":"Ada"}`. Object keys come out in the map's key order.

Records become objects with their fields in declaration order, tuples become arrays, and atoms, characters and constructors without a payload (`Monday`) become strings. `Just(x)` renders as `x`. Any other constructor with a payload, such as `Ok(1)`, renders as `null`, as does anything else with no JSON form, so `stringify` never fails.

entries.name: Inspectable
entries.summary:
Types that can be written out structurally, for debugging.

The output shows how the value is built: strings in quotes, `Just(...)` around an optional. Use `Showable` for text meant for users.

Every type is inspectable, so `inspected` and `IO.inspect` work on any value. A type that wants a different rendering overrides `inspectValue`.

```kex
[1, 2].inspected       # => "[1, 2]"
Just("hi").inspected   # => "Just(\"hi\")"
```

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary:
Writes the value structurally, with ANSI colors when `colors` is true.

`inspected` and `IO.inspect` call it with the console's color setting. Call it directly only to force colors on or off.

entries.name: Showable
entries.summary:
Types with a short text form for users.

Interpolation, printing and `to(String)` use `Showable`. A string shows without quotes, `Just(x)` shows as `x`, and `None` shows as an empty string. Use `Inspectable` to see a value's structure.

```kex
"hello".showValue          # => "hello"
Just("hello").showValue    # => "hello"
None.showValue             # => ""
```

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary:
Returns the value's text for users.

Implement it for a type whose useful text differs from its structure. Leave out ANSI styling: the text also goes to files and logs.

entries.name: Inspectable
entries.summary: Every type is inspectable through this structural rendering.

entries.name: Showable
entries.summary: The default text for the built-in Showable types. A type can replace it, as `Date`, `Time` and `DateTime` do.

entries.name: Result<X, E>
entries.summary:
Showing a `Result` shows what it carries, so `Ok(42)` shows as `42`, but an `Error` keeps its marker: `Error(bad)`. Without it a failure and a success would print alike.

The marker matches how an error appears inside a collection, `[1, Error(Bad(no))]`, since elements are written structurally. Inspecting a result, or matching on it, is unaffected.

entries.name: Kex
entries.summary:
The running toolchain: its backend, version and optional features.

```kex
Kex.BACKEND                  # => Interpreter
Kex.BACKEND.compiled?        # => false
Kex.VERSION.release          # => "0.4.0"
Kex.Feature.has?(Kex.FileSystem)   # => true
```

entries.name: Backend
entries.summary: The backend running the program: the tree-walking `Interpreter` or the `Beam` virtual machine.

entries.name: interpreted?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for the tree-walking interpreter.

entries.name: compiled?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a backend that runs compiled code, which today is only the BEAM.

entries.name: beam?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for the BEAM virtual machine, which the web server and clustering need.

entries.name: Feature
entries.summary:
A capability that some builds leave out. Check it with `Kex.Feature.has?` before relying on it.

`FileSystem` means the program can read and write the host's files (`FS`). `ExternalPrograms` means it can run other programs (`Process.run`, `Process.stream`); the browser build cannot.

Kex's own processes (`spawn`, `receive`) exist on every backend. Networking support is reported separately by `Net.Support.current`.

entries.name: BACKEND
entries.summary: The backend running this program. Ask it with `interpreted?`, `compiled?` or `beam?`.

entries.name: Version
entries.summary: The version of the Kex toolchain running a program, as `Kex.VERSION` holds it. `kex --version` and the REPL banner report the same numbers.

entries.name: Version
entries.summary: Versions order by release, the way semantic versioning orders them: major, minor and patch numerically, then a pre-release below its release (`0.4.0-rc.1 < 0.4.0`). The revision is build metadata and does not take part, so two builds of one release compare `Equal`.

entries.name: tuple
entries.summary: Returns the major, minor and patch numbers and the revision as a tuple, for destructuring.

entries.name: release
entries.summary: Returns the version as `0.4.0`, or `0.4.0-rc.1` for a pre-release. Version ranges are matched against this string.

entries.name: number
entries.summary: Returns `release` followed by the build revision, if there is one. This is what `kex --version` and the REPL banner print.

entries.name: compare
entries.summary:
Compares this version with `other` by release.

Pre-release channels compare one dot-separated part at a time: numeric parts numerically, below any named part; named parts as strings; and a channel that runs out first is the lower (`rc < rc.1`).

entries.name: VERSION
entries.summary: This build's version.

entries.name: LoadedModule
entries.summary:
A compiled module loaded into the running program by `Kex.load`.

It is for programs that pick their code at run time, such as a site generator rendering a theme's templates or a plugin host. Compile the source once with `kex --compile -o <dir>`, then load the `.beam` and call into it as often as needed.

Top-level declarations of `<stem>.kex` compile into the module `kex_<stem>`, in `kex_<stem>.beam`. Give each generated file a distinct name, or put its declarations inside a `module`, whose functions compile into `Kex.<Name>`.

Only the BEAM backend can load modules; under the interpreter `Kex.load` returns an `Error`.

```kex
let theme = Kex.load("cache/kex_theme_3f2a.beam").try
let html = theme.call(:render, [context]).try
```

entries.name: load
entries.summary: Loads the compiled module at `path`, replacing any older version of it already loaded. See `Kex.LoadedModule`.

entries.name: loaded
entries.summary: Returns the module already loaded under `name`, or `None`.

entries.name: call
entries.summary:
Calls the module's function `function` with `arguments`.

A failure inside the call returns an `Error` describing it, as does a function the module does not export with that many arguments. A `foul` function takes a hidden extra argument for its capabilities, so only pure functions can be called this way.

entries.name: hash
entries.summary:
Returns a non-cryptographic hash of any value, an `Integer` from 0 to 2^32 - 1 that is the same for equal values.

It is cheap to compute over a large structure, which suits noticing when data has changed. The number is stable only within one running program: it differs between the interpreter and the BEAM and may change between Kex versions, so do not store or send it. Use `Digest` for that, or where someone could choose inputs to collide.

entries.name: Kex.Feature
entries.summary: Which optional capabilities this build includes. Networking is reported separately by `Net.Support`.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when this build includes `f`.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: Returns every optional capability this build includes.

entries.name: Kex.Interface
entries.summary: Reading the typed public surface of a compiled Kex module.

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads the typed public interface stored in a compiled Kex module. Returns `None` when the file does not exist, is not a `.beam` file, or has no interface chunk.

The term is a tree of tuples, lists, atoms, integers and strings, read with pattern matching and `Tuple.items`.

entries.name: inspected
entries.summary:
Returns the structural text of any value, the form the REPL echoes.

To print a value in the middle of a pipeline, use `inspect` instead.

entries.name: inspect
entries.summary: Prints `value` and its type to stderr and returns `value` unchanged, so it can go anywhere in a pipeline. The same as `IO.inspect`.

entries.name: followedBy
signatures: followedBy(f: (A -> B), g: (B -> C)) -> A -> C
entries.summary: Returns a function that applies `f`, then `g` to what `f` returned.

entries.name: atom?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `value` is an atom, such as `:ok`. Universal: reachable on every type through UFCS, so it answers where the static type is `Any`. A `Bool`, `None` and a constructor such as `Red` are values of their own types, not atoms.

On the BEAM a constructor is spelled as an atom of its name, so an atom written like one of the program's constructors or type names (`:Red` next to `type Color = Red | Green`) answers as that constructor or type would, just as `Type.of` does. Lower-case atoms never collide.

entries.name: List
entries.summary:
An ordered, immutable sequence, written `[1, 2, 3]`.

Lists are the default collection in Kex. Every operation returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged.

```kex
let scores = [7, 2, 9, 4]
scores.filter { |n| n > 3 }      # => [7, 9, 4]
scores.sort                      # => [2, 4, 7, 9]
scores.map { |n| n * 10 }.sum    # => 220
```

Lookups that can come up empty, such as `first`, `at` and `find`, return an `Optional`:

```kex
[].first.or(0)        # => 0
[1, 2].at(9).or(0)    # => 0
```

Lists implement `Enumerable` and `Foldable`, which supply `map`, `filter`, `find`, `all?` and `reduce`.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Sums all elements. Returns `0` for an empty list.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Multiplies all elements. Returns `1` for an empty list.

entries.name: flatten
entries.summary: Flattens exactly one level of nesting.

entries.name: [X]
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> X -> A)) -> A

entries.name: first
entries.summary: Returns the first element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list is empty.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns the second element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list has fewer than two elements.

entries.name: third
entries.summary: Returns the third element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list has fewer than three elements.

entries.name: rest
entries.summary: Returns all elements after the first. Returns `[]` for an empty or single-element list.

entries.name: last
entries.summary: Returns the last element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the list is empty.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of elements. With a predicate, `count` counts only the elements that satisfy it.

entries.name: length
entries.summary: Returns the number of elements; the same as `count`, under the name `String` uses.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns how many elements satisfy `pred`.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if the list contains no elements.

entries.name: find
entries.summary: Returns the first element satisfying the predicate wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if no element matches.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if at least one element satisfies the predicate.

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if every element satisfies the predicate.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Returns the list of `f` applied to each element.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Returns the elements for which `pred` is `true`.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns the elements for which `pred` is `false`, the opposite of `filter`.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each element, in order, for its side effects.

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> X -> A)) -> A
entries.summary: Folds the list from the left: starts with `acc` and combines it with each element in turn through `f`.

entries.name: into
entries.summary: Maps each element to a list and concatenates the results.

entries.name: wrap
entries.summary: Returns the one-element list `[value]`. This is `Monad`'s `wrap`.

entries.name: with
entries.summary: Applies `f` to every pairing of an element of this list with an element of `other`, walking `other` fully for each element of this list. This is `Applicable`'s `with`.

entries.name: at
entries.summary: Returns the element at position `i` (0-based) wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the index is out of range. A negative `i` counts back from the end.

entries.name: get
entries.summary: Returns the element at position `i` (0-based), or `None` when the index is out of range; the same as `at`. Given a `Range`, `get` returns a sublist.

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary: Returns `true` if `elem` is present in the list.

entries.name: indexOf
entries.summary: Returns the first index at which `elem` appears, wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if the element is not present.

entries.name: findIndex
entries.summary: Returns the index of the first element satisfying `pred`, wrapped in `Just`, or `None` if none does. To search by value, use `indexOf`.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.summary: Returns the longest leading run of elements satisfying `pred`. Unlike `filter`, it stops at the first element that fails, so matches after that point are left out.

entries.name: dropWhile
entries.summary: Returns everything from the first element that fails `pred` onwards: the part `takeWhile` leaves.

entries.name: uniq
entries.summary: Returns the list with duplicates removed, keeping the first occurrence of each element.

entries.name: partition
entries.summary: Splits the list into two lists: those for which `pred` is `true` (first) and those for which it is `false` (second).

entries.name: collect
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and keeps the unwrapped `Just` results, dropping each `None`. It filters and maps in one pass.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` elements.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary: Returns the list without its first `n` elements.

entries.name: slice
entries.summary:
Returns the sublist of `length` elements starting at index `start`, counting from 0.

Out-of-range windows are clamped, as with `take` and `drop`. A start past the end gives `[]`, a length running past the end stops there, and a negative length gives `[]`. A negative start counts back from the end, as in Ruby, so `-1` is the last element; a start that is still before the beginning gives `[]`.

entries.name: push
entries.summary: Returns the list with `x` appended at the end.

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary: Returns the elements in reverse order.

entries.name: zip
entries.summary: Pairs each element of this list with the corresponding element of `other`. Stops at the end of the shorter list.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted in ascending natural order.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted by a comparator, which returns `true` when its first argument belongs before its second.

entries.name: min
entries.summary: Returns the smallest element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list. Elements compare in the same natural order `sort` uses.

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the largest element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list. Elements compare in the same natural order `sort` uses.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and multiplies the results.

entries.name: minBy
entries.summary: Returns the element with the smallest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list. The first of several tying elements wins.

entries.name: maxBy
entries.summary: Returns the element with the largest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list. The first of several tying elements wins.

entries.name: sortBy
entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted by the key `f` gives each one, smallest key first. The sort is stable: elements with equal keys keep their order.

entries.name: groupBy
entries.summary: Groups the elements by the key `f` gives each one. Each group keeps its elements in their original order.

entries.name: tally
entries.summary: Counts how many times each distinct element occurs.

entries.name: slices
entries.summary: Splits the list into consecutive pieces of `n` elements; the last piece holds whatever is left over. Ruby calls this `each_slice`.

entries.name: windows
entries.summary: Returns every run of `n` consecutive elements, each overlapping the next by all but one element. Ruby calls this `each_cons`.

entries.name: difference
entries.summary: Returns the elements of this list that are not in `other`, in order. Duplicates in this list are kept unless `other` removes them.

entries.name: intersect
entries.summary: Returns the distinct elements present in both lists, in this list's order.

entries.name: union
entries.summary: Returns the distinct elements of both lists, this list's first and then the new ones from `other`.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and sums the results.

entries.name: join
entries.summary:
Renders the elements and concatenates them with `sep` between neighbours, or with nothing between them when no separator is given.

Elements need not be strings. Each is rendered the way string interpolation renders it.

entries.name: Map
entries.summary: The type of maps from `K` to `V`, usually written `{K: V}`.

entries.name: Map<K, V>
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>
update(key: K, f: (V -> V)) -> Map<K, V>
update(key: K, default: V, f: (V -> V)) -> Map<K, V>

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Folds over the map's `(key, value)` pairs in key order.

`Enumerable` builds `map`, `filter`, `find`, `any?` and the rest on it. The block receives the accumulator and one pair, which you destructure to get the key and value.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: Returns the empty map, the `Monoid` identity: `m.combine({})` is `m`.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Merges two maps, keeping `other`'s value when both have a key. This is the `Monoid` operation, and does the same as `merge`.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Returns the value stored under `key`, or `None` when the key is absent.

When there is a sensible fallback, `get(key, default)` returns the value unwrapped.

entries.name: put
signatures: put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with `k` mapped to `v`, replacing any previous entry for that key.

The original map is unchanged. `put!` rebinds the variable holding the map to the result.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary: Returns a new map without `key`, or the same map when `key` is not present. `delete!` rebinds the variable instead.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `key` has an entry in the map.

Unlike `get` with a default, it tells a missing key apart from a key whose value happens to equal the default.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries satisfying `pred`.

entries.name: keys
entries.summary: Returns the map's keys as a sorted list.

entries.name: values
entries.summary: Returns the map's values as a list, ordered by their keys.

entries.name: entries
entries.summary:
Returns the map's entries as a list of `(key, value)` tuples, in key order.

Use it to reach the `List` functions that maps do not have, such as `sort`.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each key and value, for its side effects.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each key and value and returns the results as a list.

The result is a list, not a map, since `f` may return anything. To get a map back, use `mapValues` or `mapKeys`.

entries.name: mapValues
entries.summary: Returns a new map with every value replaced by `f(value)`. The keys are left alone.

entries.name: mapKeys
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with every key replaced by `f(key)`. The values are left alone.

If `f` maps two keys to the same result, the entry whose original key sorts last wins.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Returns a map of the entries for which `pred` returns `true`. Unlike `map`, it returns a map.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns a map of the entries for which `pred` returns `false`, the opposite of `filter`.

entries.name: merge
entries.summary: Returns a new map holding the entries of both. When a key appears in both, `other`'s value wins, which makes it the way to lay overrides on top of defaults.

entries.name: update
signatures: update(key: K, f: (V -> V)) -> Map<K, V>
update(key: K, default: V, f: (V -> V)) -> Map<K, V>
entries.summary: Replaces the value under `key` with `f` applied to it. A missing key stays missing; to start from a value, pass a default as the second argument.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when at least one entry satisfies `pred`.

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when every entry satisfies `pred`, and `true` for the empty map.

entries.name: find
entries.summary: Returns the first entry, in key order, that satisfies `pred` as a `(key, value)` tuple, or `None` when nothing matches.

entries.name: none?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when no entry satisfies `pred`.

entries.name: one?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when exactly one entry satisfies `pred`.

entries.name: matching
entries.summary: The entries `pred` holds for, as (key, value) pairs.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries. It is `empty?` under the `Blankable` name, so generic code can test maps as it tests strings and lists.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Builds a map from `(key, value)` pairs. A key that appears more than once keeps its last value. Ruby calls this `to_h`.

entries.name: Math
entries.summary:
Mathematical constants and functions.

Angles are in radians. Every function takes a `Number`, an `Integer` or a `Float`, and all but `abs`, `floor` and `ceil` return a `Float`.

A Kex `Float` is always finite. A result with no real value (`Math.sqrt(-1.0)`) or one too large for a float (`Math.exp(1000.0)`) raises an error; there is no `NaN` or `Infinity` to check for.

```kex
Math.sqrt(2.0)              # => 1.4142135623730951
Math.hypot(3.0, 4.0)        # => 5.0
Math.sin(Math.PI / 2.0)     # => 1.0
```

`abs`, `floor`, `ceil` and `sqrt` can also be called on the number, which reads better in a chain: `x.abs` rather than `Math.abs(x)`. `round` exists only in that form.

entries.name: PI
entries.summary: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.

entries.name: E
entries.summary: The base of the natural logarithm.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root of `x`. Raises an error for a negative `x`.

entries.name: cbrt
entries.summary: Returns the cube root of `x`, which may be negative.

entries.name: sin
entries.summary: Returns the sine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: cos
entries.summary: Returns the cosine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: tan
entries.summary: Returns the tangent of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: asin
entries.summary: Returns the arc sine of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

entries.name: acos
entries.summary: Returns the arc cosine of `x` in radians, in the range 0 to π.

entries.name: atan
entries.summary:
Returns the arc tangent of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

To turn a vector into an angle, use `atan2`, which also finds the right quadrant.

entries.name: atan2
entries.summary:
Returns the angle of the vector `(x, y)` in radians, from -π to π.

The signs of both components decide the quadrant, which `atan` cannot do. `y` comes first.

entries.name: deg2Rad
entries.summary: Converts an angle from degrees to radians, the unit the trigonometric functions take.

entries.name: rad2Deg
entries.summary: Converts an angle from radians to degrees, the inverse of `deg2Rad`.

entries.name: sinh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic sine of `x`.

entries.name: cosh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of `x`.

entries.name: tanh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of `x`, always between -1 and 1.

entries.name: log
entries.summary:
Returns the natural logarithm of `x`, or with `base` the logarithm to that base.

Raises an error when `x` is zero or negative.

entries.name: log2
entries.summary: Returns the base-2 logarithm of `x`, like `Math.log(x, 2.0)`.

entries.name: log10
entries.summary: Returns the base-10 logarithm of `x`.

entries.name: exp
entries.summary:
Returns `e` raised to the power `x`, the inverse of `Math.log`.

Raises an error when the result is too large for a float, which happens just past `x` of 709.

entries.name: pow
entries.summary:
Returns `x` raised to the power `y`.

The result is a `Float` even for whole numbers. For an exact integer power use `Integer.pow`: `2.pow(100)` keeps every digit, and `Math.pow(2, 100)` does not.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary:
Returns `x` without its sign, as the same type: an `Integer` stays an `Integer`.

`x.abs` does the same.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns `x` rounded down to an integer, toward negative infinity.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns `x` rounded up to an integer, toward positive infinity.

entries.name: hypot
entries.summary: Returns +sqrt(x*x + y*y)+, without overflowing for large `x` or `y`.

entries.name: Reader
entries.summary: A read hook for `Mock.Files`: returns a path's content, or `None` for no such file.

entries.name: Lookup
entries.summary: A lookup hook for `Mock.Env`: returns a variable's value, or `None` for unset.

entries.name: Tick
entries.summary: A hook for `Mock.Clock` that returns the current instant.

entries.name: Writer
entries.summary:
A write hook for `Mock.Env`, called with the name and value a program set.

Writes under a `Mock.Env` never reach the real environment, and the record cannot change, so this hook is the only way to see them. An `unset` arrives as the name with an empty value. Without a hook, writes are dropped.

entries.name: Mock
signatures: input(first: String, second: String, third: String, fourth: String) -> Void

entries.name: Files
entries.summary:
A read-only stand-in for the `FS.File` capability, for `with FS.File = ...`.

It holds no global state and ends with its block. Every write, delete, copy and open fails, so a test that writes a file and reads it back needs `Mock.FS`.

```kex
with FS.File = Mock.Files { files: {"kex.toml": "name = \"demo\""} } do
  assert(loadConfig() == "demo")
end
```

Set `onRead` to compute the answer, for example from the path. When it is set, `files` is not consulted, and its `None` means no such file.

entries.name: Env
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `ENV` capability, for `with ENV = ...`.

A name not in `vars` reads as unset. Set `onGet` to compute values instead, and `onSet` to see what the program writes.

```kex
with ENV = Mock.Env { vars: {"HOME": "/fake"} } do
  assert(configHome() == "/fake/.config")
end
```

entries.name: Clock
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `Time.Clock` capability, for `with Time.Clock = ...`. Inside the block, `Time.now`, `Date.today` and `DateTime.utcNow` read from it.

```kex
with Time.Clock = Mock.Clock { at: DateTime.parse("2026-07-30T14:03:00Z").try } do
  assert(Date.today().iso == "2026-07-30")
end
```

The clock is frozen at `at`, zone included, so `Date.today()` is the date in the zone you wrote, not the zone of the machine running the test.

A frozen clock makes every measured interval zero. For a clock that runs, set `onNow`: a block uses the clock of the place it was written, so one written outside the `with` reads the real clock.

```kex
with Time.Clock = Mock.Clock { onNow: Just({ DateTime.now() + 3.day }) } do
  let started = DateTime.epochNanos()
  runTheThing()
  assert(DateTime.epochNanos() > started)
end
```

entries.name: Mock.FS
entries.summary:
A global stand-in for the filesystem: files a test declares here are what the real `FS.File` reads.

The store lasts until `clear`, so clear it in an `after` hook or the next test sees the same files.

```kex
describe "the config loader" do
  before do
    Mock.FS.files({ "app.conf": "port = 8080\n" })
  end

  after do
    Mock.FS.clear()
  end

  it "reads the port" do
    Assert.equal(loadPort(), 8080)
  end
end
```

entries.name: File
entries.summary: Declares one file and its content.

entries.name: Directory
entries.summary: Declares a directory at `path`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Empties the store, removing every file and directory declared so far.

Call it in an `after` hook, since the store is shared by every test.

entries.name: files
entries.summary: Declares several files at once, from a map of paths to contents (the shape `Mock.Files` takes).

entries.name: onRead
entries.summary:
Serves reads from `reader` in place of the declared files.

Use it when the content depends on the path. While it is set, files declared with `File` or `files` are not read, and `None` from `reader` means no such file.

entries.name: Mock.ENV
entries.summary:
A global overlay on the process environment, so a test decides what `ENV` holds.

The overlay lasts until `clear`, so clear it in an `after` hook.

```kex
Mock.ENV.vars({ "HOME": "/fake", "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" })
assert(configPath() == "/fake/.config")
Mock.ENV.clear()
```

entries.name: set
entries.summary: Sets one variable in the overlay.

entries.name: unset
entries.summary: Makes a variable read as unset, whatever the real environment holds.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary: Removes the whole overlay, restoring the real environment.

entries.name: vars
entries.summary:
Declares the whole overlay in one call.

To compute values per lookup, use `with ENV = Mock.Env { onGet: ... }`.

entries.name: Mock.IO
signatures: input(first: String, second: String, third: String, fourth: String) -> Void
entries.summary:
A global stand-in for the console: it captures what a program prints and feeds it lines as if they had been typed.

```kex
Mock.IO.start()
Mock.IO.input("Ada", "42")
greet()
Assert.equal(Mock.IO.output(), "hello, Ada\n")
Mock.IO.stop()
```

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Starts capturing output and serving queued input.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops capturing, and restores the real console.

entries.name: output
entries.summary:
Returns everything the program has printed since capturing started.

Newlines are included, so a single `IO.printLine("hi")` gives `"hi\n"`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Discards the output captured so far and keeps capturing.

Use it between phases of a test when only the later output matters.

entries.name: input
signatures: input(first: String, second: String, third: String, fourth: String) -> Void
entries.summary:
Queues the lines `IO.getLine` will return, in order.

Takes a list, or up to four lines as separate arguments. Calls add to the queue. Once it is empty, `IO.getLine` returns `None` and `IO.readLine` returns `Ok(None)`, as at the end of real input.

entries.name: cannedRead
entries.summary: Named apart from `read`: `this.read(path)` would bind to the capability's own `read : FilePath -> String?`, not to this function.

entries.name: open
entries.summary: A fake is a value, so there is nowhere for a write to go. Failing lets a test that did not expect a write notice it.

entries.name: lookup
entries.summary: Named apart from `get`: `this.get(key)` would bind to the capability's own `get`, not to this function.

entries.name: set
entries.summary: A write goes to `onSet` or is dropped. It must not reach the real environment, where it would leak into later tests and into every process the suite starts, and `vars` cannot change.

entries.name: Mock.Net
entries.summary: Scripted inputs for testing HTTP, DNS, sockets and WebSockets.

entries.name: Mock.Net.HTTP
entries.summary: Scripted HTTP responses.

entries.name: Transport
entries.summary: Responses a scripted transport returns, in order.

entries.name: Mock.Net.DNS
entries.summary: Scripted DNS answers.

entries.name: ResolverScript
entries.summary: The addresses each hostname resolves to.

entries.name: Mock.Net.Socket
entries.summary: Scripted socket data.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: Chunks delivered in order as incoming socket data.

entries.name: Mock.Net.WebSocket
entries.summary: Scripted WebSocket messages.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: Messages a scripted connection delivers, in order.

entries.name: Net
entries.summary:
Networking values shared by the network modules: ports, a report of which transports this build supports, and the error type they all return.

```kex
using Net

let https = Port.from(443).try
if Support.current.tls.usable? then https.string else "TLS unavailable" end
```

entries.name: Port
entries.summary:
A TCP or UDP port number, checked to be in `0..65535`.

Build one with `Port.from`. Port zero asks the operating system for a free port where a listening API allows it; after binding, ask the server or socket which port it got.

entries.name: SupportValue
entries.summary:
Whether a networking feature is built in, and whether it can be used here.

`compiled?` describes the build. `usable?` also takes the running environment into account: a browser build can contain an HTTP client while browser policy still blocks a lower-level transport.

entries.name: SupportReport
entries.summary:
The networking features of the running build, one `SupportValue` each.

Consult it to pick a transport at run time. A program that needs one feature can check that field at startup and stop with a clear message. The tree-walk interpreter (`kex -R`) reports every feature as unavailable.

entries.name: Net.Port
entries.summary: Construction of `Port` values.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Returns `value` as a `Port`, or a `Parse` error when it is outside `0..65535`.

entries.name: Net.Support
entries.summary: Run-time discovery of the optional network transports and protocols.

entries.name: current
entries.summary: Returns which networking features this build contains and which are usable now.

entries.name: NetOperation
entries.summary: The subsystem or operation that produced a networking error.

entries.name: NetErrorKind
entries.summary: The category of a networking failure, the same on every backend.

entries.name: NetError
entries.summary:
The error every network module returns.

Branch on `kind`; it does not change between backends. `message` is text for a person and may differ by backend. `phase` names the protocol step that failed, such as a TLS handshake, and `progress` counts the bytes transferred before an operation failed partway.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the port number as decimal text, with no host or scheme.

entries.name: Node
signatures: send(node: Atom, name: Atom, message: X) -> Void
entries.summary:
Distributed Kex: this BEAM node and the nodes it is connected to.

A node is a running BEAM VM with a name. Once two nodes with the same cookie are connected, a `Process` from one works on the other: `send`, `link`, `monitor` and `Server` handles all work across the network.

Name a node when starting it (`kex --sname a --cookie secret app.kex`), or from inside the program with `Node.start`:

```kex
using Node

main do
  Node.connect(:b@myhost)
  Node.send(:b@myhost, :logger, (:hello, Node.self))
end
```

Node names are atoms: `:b@myhost` for a short name, a quoted `:"b@host.example.com"` for one with dots, or `Atom.from(text)` for one built at run time.

Plain data (numbers, strings, lists, tuples, records) can be sent anywhere. A message that carries a function, such as a lambda, needs the same compiled code on both nodes; `Node.spawn` sends its block's code along.

Under the tree-walk interpreter (`kex -R`) the program is always a single node with no name.

entries.name: self
entries.summary: Returns this node's name, or `:nonode@nohost` when it is not distributed.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when this node has a name, so other nodes can connect to it.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: Returns the nodes this one is connected to, not including itself.

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Makes this node distributed under `name`, as `--sname` or `--name` would at startup. A name whose host has a dot (`:"app@host.example.com"`) uses long names; any other uses short names.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops distribution: the node drops its name and every connection.

entries.name: connect
entries.summary: Connects to the node named `node`. Both nodes must share a cookie.

entries.name: disconnect
entries.summary: Drops the connection to `node`.

entries.name: setCookie
entries.summary: Sets the cookie this node presents when connecting. Nodes connect only when their cookies match.

entries.name: send
signatures: send(node: Atom, name: Atom, message: X) -> Void
entries.summary:
Sends `message` to the process registered as `name` on `node`.

Like `Process.send`, it does not block and does not fail, even when no such process exists.

entries.name: whereIs
entries.summary: Returns the process registered as `name` on `node`, or `None`.

entries.name: spawn
entries.summary:
Runs `block` in a new process on `node` and returns it.

When `node` has not loaded the module the block belongs to, that module's compiled code is sent and loaded first. A module `node` already has is not replaced.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Whole numbers, of arbitrary size.

`Integer` has no width limit, so a factorial or a cryptographic modulus is an `Integer` like any other.

`Integer` and `Float` compare and sort together: `0 == 0.0` is `true` and `[1, 2.5, 3].sort` works. Their arithmetic differs. `/` on two integers is integer division, and `sqrt` always returns a `Float`.

```kex
7 / 2          # => 3      (integer division)
7.0 / 2.0      # => 3.5
16.sqrt        # => 4.0    (a Float, even from an Integer)
(-7).modulo(3) # => 2      (mathematical modulo, not C remainder)
```

entries.name: even?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is divisible by two. Zero is even, and negative numbers follow the same rule.

entries.name: odd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is not divisible by two. The opposite of `even?`.

entries.name: dividesBy?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the integer divides evenly by `n`.

Zero is divisible by every non-zero integer. Nothing is divisible by zero, not even zero.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the integer, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary:
Returns the square root as a `Float`.

The result is a `Float` even when the root is exact. Round or floor it to get an integer back.

entries.name: modulo
entries.summary:
Returns `this` modulo `n`.

The result takes the sign of `n`, unlike the C-style remainder, so `(-1).modulo(3)` is `2`. That makes it the one to use for wrapping an index that may have gone negative.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: times
entries.summary:
Calls `f` exactly `this` times, passing the 0-based iteration index.

When the loop is about the numbers themselves, `(1..n).each` often reads better.

entries.name: downTo
entries.summary: Returns the range from this integer down to `last`, both included, counting by -1. It is empty when `last` is larger.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged, so code that floors a `Number` works on integers too.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.ceil`.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.round`.

entries.name: pow
entries.summary:
Raises the integer to an integer power, exactly. `2.pow(100)` is the whole 31-digit number; `Math.pow` returns a `Float`.

A negative exponent gives the reciprocal truncated toward zero, as `/` does: `0` for any base but `1` and `-1`.

entries.name: div
entries.summary: Divides and rounds toward negative infinity, the quotient that goes with `modulo`. Plain `/` truncates toward zero, so the two differ when the signs differ. Ruby's `/` on integers behaves like this one.

entries.name: divmod
entries.summary: Returns the floored quotient and the `modulo` remainder together, so +q * n + r == this+ always holds.

entries.name: gcd
entries.summary: Returns the greatest common divisor, never negative. `0.gcd(0)` is `0`.

entries.name: lcm
entries.summary: Returns the least common multiple, never negative. It is `0` when either integer is zero.

entries.name: digits
entries.summary: Returns the decimal digits of the integer's magnitude, least significant first, as Ruby's `digits` does. `.reverse` gives reading order.

entries.name: zero?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for zero.

entries.name: positive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the number is greater than zero.

entries.name: negative?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the number is less than zero.

entries.name: countTo
entries.summary: `times` when compiled: `block` applied to each index from this one up to `limit`, a recursion the specialize-blocks pass copies into the caller with the block in place.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary:
Double-precision floating-point numbers.

A Kex `Float` is always finite. An operation that would produce `NaN` or `Infinity` raises, so there is no `nan?` to check for.

`Float` and `Integer` compare and sort together; see `Integer`.

```kex
3.7.floor      # => 3
3.7.round      # => 4
(-3.7).toInteger  # => -3   (truncates toward zero)
```

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the float, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root. Raises for a negative float.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the float falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the largest integer not greater than the float. It rounds toward negative infinity, so for negative values it differs from `toInteger`.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the smallest integer not less than the float.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the nearest integer, with halves rounding away from zero.

entries.name: toInteger
entries.summary: Drops the fractional part and returns an `Integer`. For negative values this differs from `floor`.

entries.name: zero?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for zero.

entries.name: positive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the number is greater than zero.

entries.name: negative?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the number is less than zero.

entries.name: Integer
signatures: parse(text: String, radix: Integer = …, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Integer, ParseError<Integer>>
entries.summary:
Reading integers out of text.

`"42".to(Integer)` returns an `Optional`. Use `parse` when the caller needs to know why the text is not a number: its `ParseError` has one case per reason.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(text: String, radix: Integer = …, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Integer, ParseError<Integer>>
entries.summary:
Parses `text` as an integer: an optional sign, then digits in `radix`. Group separators must follow `culture`'s grouping; digits with no separator read in every culture.

A number followed by other text is a `Trailing` error carrying the number and the rest, so matching on it reads a number off the front of `"10 USD"`.

entries.name: Float
signatures: parse(text: String, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Float, ParseError<Float>>
entries.summary: Reading floating-point numbers out of text.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(text: String, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Float, ParseError<Float>>
entries.summary: Parses `text` as a float: an optional sign, digits (grouped by `culture`'s rules if separators appear), an optional decimal part after the culture's decimal separator, and an optional exponent (`e3`, `E-2`). A whole number parses too: `"5"` gives `5.0`.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary:
The largest finite `Float`.

Kex has no float infinity, so this is the starting value for a running minimum.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite `Float`, `-Float.MAX`. Some languages use MIN for the smallest positive float; Kex does not.

entries.name: Float32
entries.summary: The range of a 32-bit float. As for every sized float type, `MIN` is the most negative finite value.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Float32: 3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float32: -3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: Float64
entries.summary: The range of a 64-bit float, the same as a `Float`.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float64: -1.7976931348623157e308.

entries.name: Int8
entries.summary: The range of a signed 8-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int8: 127.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int8: -128.

entries.name: Int16
entries.summary: The range of a signed 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int16: 32767.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int16: -32768.

entries.name: Int32
entries.summary: The range of a signed 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int32: 2147483647.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int32: -2147483648.

entries.name: Int64
entries.summary: The range of a signed 64-bit integer.

entries.name: UInt8
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 8-bit integer: `UInt8` is another name for `Byte`.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt8: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt8: 0.

entries.name: UInt16
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt16: 65535.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt16: 0.

entries.name: UInt32
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt32: 4294967295.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt32: 0.

entries.name: UInt64
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 64-bit integer.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt64: 0.

entries.name: Byte
entries.summary: The range of a `Byte`, Kex's unsigned 8-bit integer (also called `UInt8`).

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Byte: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Byte: 0.

entries.name: Number
signatures: parse(text: String, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Number, ParseError<Number>>
entries.summary: Reading a number from text that may hold either an integer or a float, and writing numbers by a digit pattern.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(text: String, culture: Culture = …) -> Result<Number, ParseError<Number>>
entries.summary:
Parses `text` as an `Integer` or a `Float`, whichever it describes. A fraction or an exponent makes it a `Float`; otherwise the grammar is `Float.parse`'s.

Use it for input such as a config value or a CSV column that may hold either kind.

entries.name: format
entries.summary:
Builds a `NumberFormat` from a digit pattern, for `to(String, format)`.

The pattern is checked during compilation, so a bad pattern is a build error.

- `0` is a required digit: `000` pads the integer part to three digits,
  and `.00` always writes two decimals.
- `#` is an optional digit: `#.##` writes at most two decimals and drops
  trailing zeros. Optional digits come before required ones in the
  integer part (`#0`) and after them in the decimals (`.0#`).
- `.` starts the decimals. The value is rounded to as many decimals as
  the pattern allows, with ties away from zero.

The integer part always has at least one digit, so `#.00` writes `0.50`, never `.50`. A value that rounds to zero has no minus sign.

entries.name: validateFormat
entries.summary: Checks a `Number.format` pattern during compilation and reports the first character that does not fit.

entries.name: NumberFormat
entries.summary: A digit pattern such as `"#.00"` for `to(String, format)`; the patterns are described at `Number.format`. Build one with `Number.format`, which checks the pattern during compilation, or with `NumberFormat.parse` for a pattern known only at run time.

entries.name: NumberFormat
signatures: layout(pattern: String) -> Result<(Integer, Integer, Integer), (Integer, String)>

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Checks a digit pattern known only at run time and returns it as a `NumberFormat`. `Number.format` describes the patterns.

entries.name: layout
signatures: layout(pattern: String) -> Result<(Integer, Integer, Integer), (Integer, String)>
entries.summary: Returns what a pattern writes: the fewest integer digits, the fewest decimals and the most decimals. For a bad pattern it returns the index of the first problem and a message.

entries.name: Number
signatures: to(String: Type, format: NumberFormat, culture: Culture) -> String?

entries.name: to
signatures: to(String: Type, format: NumberFormat, culture: Culture) -> String?
entries.summary: Writes the number by a digit pattern, described at `Number.format`.

entries.name: leadingZeros
entries.summary: `text` with leading zeros up to `width` characters.

entries.name: trailingZeros
entries.summary: `text` with exactly `width` characters if it is shorter, or with its trailing zeros dropped down to `width` characters if it is longer.

entries.name: OptionKind
entries.summary:
The kind of value an option takes.

`StringValue` takes any text, `IntegerValue` takes a whole number, and `FlagValue` takes no value and reads as `"true"` when given.

entries.name: OptionSpec
entries.summary: One declared option. The `OptionConfig` builders make these, so you rarely write one yourself.

entries.name: CommandHandler
entries.summary: The function that runs a command. It gets the parsed options with the command's own words removed from `arguments`, so `tey add greet` passes `["greet"]`, and returns the process exit code.

entries.name: CommandSpec
entries.summary: One declared command. The `OptionConfig.command` builders make these.

entries.name: OptionConfig
entries.summary:
A tool's whole command-line interface: its name, its options, and its commands.

Start one with `OptionParser.define` and chain `string`, `integer`, `flag` and `command` onto it. Each returns a new `OptionConfig`.

entries.name: ParsedOptions
entries.summary: The result of a successful parse: the option values, and the words that were not options.

entries.name: OptionParseError
entries.summary:
Why a command line could not be parsed.

`OptionParser.errorMessage` turns one into a message for the user, and `OptionConfig.run` prints that message for you.

entries.name: value
entries.summary: Returns the value given for the option named `name`, or `None` when it was neither supplied nor defaulted.

entries.name: flagEnabled?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the flag named `name` was given.

entries.name: integerValue
entries.summary:
Returns the value of an integer option as an `Integer`, or `None` when it is absent or does not parse.

An option declared with `integer` is checked during parsing, so for one of those `None` means the option was absent.

entries.name: OptionConfig
signatures: string(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
integer(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
flag(long: String, short: Char?, description: String) -> OptionConfig
command(name: String, usage: String, description: String, section: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
passthroughCommand(name: String, usage: String, description: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig

entries.name: string
signatures: string(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary: Declares an option that takes a text value.

entries.name: integer
signatures: integer(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares an option that takes a whole number.

A value that is not a whole number fails the parse with `InvalidInteger`, so a handler never sees one. Read the value with `ParsedOptions.integerValue`.

entries.name: flag
signatures: flag(long: String, short: Char?, description: String) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares an option that takes no value.

It is `"false"` unless given, then `"true"`; read it with `ParsedOptions.flagEnabled?`. Giving it a value, as in `--verbose=yes`, is an `UnexpectedValue` error.

`run` prints the help text when a flag named `help` is set, and declares no such flag itself.

entries.name: command
signatures: command(name: String, usage: String, description: String, section: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares a command and the function that runs it.

A command name may be several words (`"docs build"`); the longest match wins, so a group and its subcommands can both be declared. The handler gets the parsed options without the command's own words, and returns the process exit code.

entries.name: passthroughCommand
signatures: passthroughCommand(name: String, usage: String, description: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares a command that parses its own options.

Everything after the command's name reaches the handler unchanged in `arguments`, including options this tool also declares. Use it for a subcommand with its own `OptionConfig`. With a plain `command`, an option that both declare is taken by the outer tool and the subcommand never sees it, without any error.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `args` into option values and leftover words, without dispatching to a command.

Use it when the tool has no commands, or to look at the result before deciding what to do. `run` parses and dispatches in one call.

entries.name: run
entries.summary:
Parses `args`, runs the command they name, and returns its exit code.

Pass the result to `System.exit`.

A parse error or an unknown command prints the error and the help text to stderr and returns 1. A set `help` flag, or no arguments at all, prints the help and returns 0.

entries.name: printHelp
entries.summary:
Prints the help text and returns 0, the exit code for a successful run.

`run` calls it when the `help` flag is set. Call it yourself when the tool should show its help for some other reason.

entries.name: help
entries.summary:
Returns the tool's help text: its name and description, its options, and its commands grouped by section.

`run` and `printHelp` print it to stdout; use this to send it elsewhere. It is coloured with `Console` escapes, which are empty under `--no-colors` and `KEX_COLORS=0`.

entries.name: define
entries.summary:
Returns an empty `OptionConfig` for a tool, to chain options and commands onto.

`name` and `description` head the help text.

entries.name: commandLabel
entries.summary: Returns the label a command is listed under in the help text: its name, followed by its usage when it has one.

entries.name: commandFor
entries.summary:
Finds the declared command whose words open `arguments`, and returns it with whatever is left after them.

The command with the most words wins, so `"docs build"` is chosen over a `"docs"` that also exists. Returns `None` when no command matches.

entries.name: passthrough?
entries.summary:
Returns whether the command that `arguments` names is a passthrough command.

Returns `false` while no command matches, so options before the command word still belong to this parser.

entries.name: opensWith?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `arguments` begins with the words of `name`.

This is the test `commandFor` uses: `"docs build"` opens `["docs", "build", "src"]` but not `["docs"]`.

entries.name: errorMessage
entries.summary:
Returns a parse error as a message for the user.

`OptionConfig.run` uses it. Call it when you handle a `parse` result yourself.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `args` against a list of option and command specs.

`OptionConfig.parse` calls this; use that instead.

entries.name: Optional
entries.summary:
An optional value: `Just(x)` carries a value, `None` says there is none.

`X?` is shorthand for `Optional<X>` and is the usual spelling. Kex has no `null`; a function that may have nothing to return returns an `Optional`, and the caller has to decide what happens when it is empty. Usually that is an `.or(default)` at the end of a chain.

When a default is not enough, match on the two cases:

entries.name: Result
entries.summary:
The outcome of an operation that can fail: `Ok(x)` on success, `Error(e)` on failure with a reason.

Use `Result` when the caller needs to know why something failed, and `Optional` when it only needs to know whether it did. `"12x".to(Integer)` returns `None`, while `Integer.parse("12x")` returns `Error(Trailing(12, "x"))`, which says where parsing stopped and on what.

entries.name: Either
entries.summary:
One of two values, of possibly different types: `Left(l)` or `Right(r)`.

Neither side means failure, as `Error` does in a `Result`. Use `Either` for a value that can take one of two shapes.

entries.name: Optionable
entries.summary:
A value that may be absent. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any optional value.

The trait requires only `set?` and `or`. It does not require `map`, because the result type of `map` differs between implementers (`Y?` for an `Optional`, `Result<Y, E>` for a `Result`), and expressing that would need a higher-kinded type parameter, which Kex does not have.

entries.name: set?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when a value is present.

Every `Optionable` type must define it; `none?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary: Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

entries.name: Resultable
entries.summary: A value that either succeeded or failed with a reason. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any result value.

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for a success.

Every `Resultable` type must define it; `error?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary: Returns the success value, or `default` on failure.

entries.name: Eitherable
entries.summary: One of two values, neither meaning failure. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any either value.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Applies `onLeft` to a `Left` or `onRight` to a `Right` and returns the result.

Every `Eitherable` type must define it. The trait requires this, and not `left?` or `right?`, because those only say which side a value is on; `either` also hands over the value.

entries.name: Optional<X>
signatures: with(other: Y?, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Z?

entries.name: set?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when a value is present.

entries.name: none?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when there is no value; the opposite of `set?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

This is the usual way to end a chain of optional steps: the code after `.or` works with a plain value.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the wrapped value and wraps the result. On `None`, `f` is not called and `None` is returned.

entries.name: into
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns an optional, and returns its result.

Use it for a step that can come up empty: `map` would give a nested `Just(Just(x))`. Once a step returns `None`, the later steps do not run.

entries.name: with
signatures: with(other: Y?, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Z?
entries.summary: Applies `f` to this value and `other`'s when both are present, and returns `None` otherwise. This is `Applicable`'s `with`.

entries.name: wrap
entries.summary: Returns `Just(value)`. This is `Monad`'s `wrap`.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Keeps the value only when `pred` accepts it, and returns `None` otherwise.

entries.name: Result<X, E>
signatures: with(other: Result<Y, E>, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Result<Z, E>

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Ok`.

entries.name: error?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Error`; the opposite of `ok?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the `Ok` value, or `default` when the result is an `Error`.

The error is discarded. To report why it failed, match on the result.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the `Ok` value. An `Error` is returned as it is, and `f` is not called.

entries.name: into
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns a `Result`, and returns its result.

Use it to chain steps that can each fail. The first `Error` ends the chain and is what the chain returns.

entries.name: with
signatures: with(other: Result<Y, E>, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Result<Z, E>
entries.summary: Applies `f` to this success and `other`'s, or returns the first error. This is `Applicable`'s `with`.

entries.name: optional
entries.summary:
Converts the result to an `Optional`, dropping the error.

Use it when the caller only cares whether there is a value, or the code that follows works with optionals.

entries.name: mapError
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the error and leaves a success alone; `map` for the error side.

entries.name: error
entries.summary: Returns the error wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for a success; the counterpart of `optional`.

entries.name: Result<_, E>
entries.summary: Makes `Result` a `Functor`, `Bindable`, `Monad` and `Applicable` over its success value, with the error type `E` fixed. The `map` and `into` above are the ones these traits use.

entries.name: wrap
entries.summary: Returns `Ok(value)`. This is `Monad`'s `wrap`.

entries.name: Validation
entries.summary:
The outcome of several independent checks: `Valid` with the value, or `Invalid` with every failure. Combining +Result+s stops at the first error; combining +Validation+s with `with` collects all of them, so a form or a config file can report every problem at once:

```kex
let checkedName(name: String) -> Validation<String, String> do
  return name.empty? then Invalid(["name is empty"]) else Valid(name)
end

checkedName("").with(checkedEmail("x")) do |n, e|
  Signup { name: n, email: e }
end
# => Invalid(["name is empty", "email has no @"])
```

`Validation` is `Applicable` but not a `Monad`. A chained step needs the previous value, which a failure does not have, so chaining could only stop at the first failure.

entries.name: Validation<X, E>
signatures: with(other: Validation<Y, E>, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Validation<Z, E>

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the value when valid, and leaves the failures of an `Invalid` as they are.

entries.name: with
signatures: with(other: Validation<Y, E>, f: (X -> Y -> Z)) -> Validation<Z, E>
entries.summary: Applies `f` to this value and `other`'s when both are valid. Otherwise it returns the failures of both, this one's first. This is `Applicable`'s `with`.

entries.name: toResult
entries.summary: Converts to a `Result`: `Ok` with the value, or `Error` with the list of failures.

entries.name: wrap
entries.summary: Returns `Valid(value)`. This is `Applicable`'s `wrap`.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(value: A, t: Type<T>, radix: Integer) -> T?
entries.summary:
Converts `value` to the type `t`, or `None` if it cannot be represented.

Pass the type name itself as `t`: `String`, `Integer`, `Float`, `List`. Conversion to `String` uses `showValue`, so it works for every value.

Most failed conversions need no explanation, so `to` returns an `Optional`. When you need to know where a parse gave up and on what, use `Integer.parse` or `Float.parse`, which return a `Result` with a `ParseError`.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Applies `onLeft` to a `Left` or `onRight` to a `Right` and returns the result.

Use it to turn an `Either` into one value without a `match`. Both functions return the same type `A`.

entries.name: left?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Left`.

entries.name: right?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Right`; the opposite of `left?`.

entries.name: Parsing
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parser combinators, for reading a text format you define yourself.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Parsing`.

An `Input` is an immutable cursor over a string. A parser takes one and returns the value it read with an advanced cursor, or a `ParseError` saying where it stopped. After a failure the caller still has the cursor it started with, so it can try something else from the same place.

```kex
using Parsing

main do
  let cursor = Input { input: "abc 123" }
  let word = cursor.takeWhile(~alpha?)
  let (text, rest) = word
  IO.printLine(text)              # prints: abc
  IO.printLine(rest.pos)          # prints: 3
end
```

The building blocks are `char` and `charWhen` for one character, `string` for a literal, `takeWhile` for a run, and `many` / `some` / `choice` for repetition and alternatives. The stdlib's `JSON` parser is built from them.

entries.name: ParseError
entries.summary:
Why a parser stopped, and at which position.

`Unexpected` carries the text that was found, `"EOF"` at the end of the input. `Expected` carries what the grammar wanted, as `string` reports it. `NoMatch` means no alternative of a `choice` matched.

```kex
Input { input: "abc" }.char('z')      # => Error(Unexpected("a", 0))
Input { input: "abc" }.string("abd")  # => Error(Expected("abd", 0))
```

entries.name: Input
entries.summary:
An immutable cursor over a string: the text and a position in it.

Create one with `Input { input: text }` and pass it to a parser. Every function that consumes input returns a new cursor and leaves this one where it was.

entries.name: Input
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>

entries.name: peek
entries.summary: Returns the character at the cursor without consuming it, or `None` at the end of the input.

entries.name: peekAt
entries.summary: Returns the character `offset` positions ahead of the cursor, or `None` when that is outside the input. A negative offset looks backwards.

entries.name: atEnd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the cursor has consumed the whole input. A top-level parser checks it to be sure nothing is left over.

entries.name: advance
entries.summary: Returns a cursor one character further on.

entries.name: advanceBy
entries.summary: Returns a cursor `count` characters further on.

entries.name: remaining
entries.summary: Returns the text from the cursor to the end of the input, for an error message or for code that does not take an `Input`.

entries.name: charWhen
entries.summary:
Reads one character if it satisfies `pred`.

Otherwise returns an `Unexpected` error with the character found, or `"EOF"` at the end of the input.

entries.name: char
entries.summary: Reads one specific character.

entries.name: whiteSpaces
entries.summary: Returns the cursor moved past any whitespace. With no whitespace it stays where it was, so it can go between any two tokens of a grammar.

entries.name: many
entries.summary:
Applies `f` as many times as it succeeds and collects the results.

It cannot fail: no match gives an empty list. It also stops when `f` succeeds without consuming anything.

entries.name: some
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Applies `f` once, then as many more times as it succeeds.

Unlike `many`, it fails when the first attempt fails. Use it where the grammar needs at least one match.

entries.name: string
entries.summary:
Reads an exact literal.

On a mismatch the `Expected` error names the whole literal and points at its start, not at the first character that differs.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.summary:
Reads characters while `pred` holds and returns them as a `String`.

It cannot fail: when the first character does not match, the text is empty. `many` with `charWhen` does the same but returns a list of characters.

entries.name: choice
signatures: choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Tries each parser in `alts` in turn from the same position and returns the first success.

When none matches, it returns `NoMatch` at the starting position.

entries.name: Period
entries.summary:
A span of calendar years, months and days.

February has 28 or 29 days and a year 365 or 366, so a month or a year is not a fixed number of seconds and cannot be a `Duration`. A `Period` keeps the calendar fields, and adding it to a date clamps the day to the end of a shorter month:

```kex
Date.of(2026, 1, 31).try + 1.month        # 2026-02-28
Date.of(2024, 2, 29).try + 1.year         # 2025-02-28
```

Use a `Duration` for elapsed time (`36.hour` is always 129600 seconds) and a `Period` for calendar steps.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
The calendar spans `1.month` and `2.year` on `Integer`.

These return a `Period`. The fixed time units (`5.second`, `90.minute`, `2.week`) return a `Duration` and live in units.kex; `4.week` is always 28 days.

entries.name: month
entries.summary: Returns a `Period` of this many calendar months.

entries.name: year
entries.summary: Returns a `Period` of this many calendar years.

entries.name: Period
signatures: of(years: Integer, months: Integer, days: Integer) -> Period
entries.summary: Constructors for `Period`.

entries.name: zero
entries.summary: Returns the empty span.

entries.name: of
signatures: of(years: Integer, months: Integer, days: Integer) -> Period
entries.summary: Returns a span of the given years, months and days.

entries.name: years
entries.summary: Returns a span of `count` calendar years.

entries.name: months
entries.summary: Returns a span of `count` calendar months.

entries.name: days
entries.summary: Returns a span of `count` calendar days.

entries.name: weeks
entries.summary: Returns a span of `count` weeks, stored as `count * 7` days.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: Returns the period's fields, for debugging output.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Returns the ISO 8601 form, which is what interpolation and `IO.printLine` show.
Returns the sum of two spans, field by field.
Returns the difference of two spans, field by field. Fields can go negative.

entries.name: negated
entries.summary: Returns the span with the sign of every field flipped.
Returns the span with every field multiplied by `factor`.

entries.name: zero?
entries.summary: Returns whether every field is zero.

entries.name: totalMonths
entries.summary:
Returns the years and months of the span as one count of months.

A year is always 12 months, while a month has no fixed number of days, so +date + span+ adds the years and months in one step and the days after.

entries.name: normalized
entries.summary:
Returns the span with whole years of months carried into `years`.

14 months becomes 1 year 2 months. Days are not carried, since a month has no fixed number of them.

entries.name: iso
entries.summary:
Returns the span as an ISO 8601 duration such as `P1Y2M3D`.

The empty span is `P0D`, because a bare `P` is not valid ISO 8601.

entries.name: Task
entries.summary:
A handle on work running in another process, whose result you can await.

Created by `Task.start`.

entries.name: Reference
entries.summary: A monitor reference, returned by `monitor` and passed back to `demonitor`.

entries.name: Process
entries.summary: A process: what `spawn` makes, what `Process.self` returns, and what `Process.whereIs` finds. `A` is the type of message it accepts, and sending it anything else is a type error. A process obtained without a declared message type takes its `A` from where it is used (`Ping(Process.self)` where a `Process<String>` is expected).

entries.name: ProcessExitReason
entries.summary: Why a process ended. The BEAM allows any term as an exit reason, so this is `Any`; the usual ones are `:normal`, `:shutdown` and application error values.

entries.name: Reply
entries.summary:
What a synchronous `slot` returns: the reply for the caller, and optionally a new state and a reason to stop.

`reply` goes back to the caller at once. A slot may leave it out only when it answers later with `from.reply(...)`. `new` is the next state; leave it out to keep the current one. `stop` ends the server after the transition. Inside a `serving X` block the checker narrows `new` from `Any?` to `X?`.

```kex
slot allowed? -> Reply<Bool> do
  let allowed = @remaining > 0
  new.remaining = allowed then @remaining - 1 else @remaining
  return { new, reply: allowed }
end

slot stop -> Reply<Integer> = { stop: :normal, reply: @remaining }
```

entries.name: From
entries.summary: A caller still waiting for its reply, for a slot that answers later. Call `reply` on it when the answer is ready.

entries.name: CallError
entries.summary: Why a call into a server failed: it timed out, the process is gone, or it crashed while handling the call.

entries.name: Server
entries.summary:
A running server and the default timeout for calls into it.

Returned by `Process.spawn`. Each `slot` in the type's `serving` block becomes a function on this `Server` that returns a `Result`.

entries.name: Process
signatures: run(command: String, args: [String], timeoutMs: Integer) -> Result<ProcessResult, String>
entries.summary: Spawning servers, running external commands, and operations on the calling process.

entries.name: spawn
entries.summary:
Starts a process running the `serving` block of `state`'s type, with `state` as its initial state, and returns a handle on it.

Each `slot` in the `serving` block becomes a function on the returned `Server`. Each returns a `Result`, because a call can time out or find the process gone.

entries.name: run
signatures: run(command: String, args: [String], timeoutMs: Integer) -> Result<ProcessResult, String>
entries.summary:
Runs an executable with a list of arguments and captures its output.

No shell is involved: nothing is glob-expanded or split on spaces, and an argument containing spaces needs no quoting. Output is read as UTF-8.

A non-zero exit status is still `Ok`; check `exitCode` on the result. `Error` means the program could not be started at all.

entries.name: stream
entries.summary:
Runs an executable connected to the caller's stdin, stdout and stderr, and returns its exit code.

Output appears as the program writes it, and a program that reads the terminal (a REPL, a password prompt) can. Nothing is captured; use `run` when you need the output as a string.

entries.name: exec
entries.summary:
Runs an executable and returns its exit code, discarding its output.

A command that could not be started gives `127`, the shell's code for "command not found". Use `run` when you need the output or must tell a failed start from a failed run.

entries.name: self
