entries.summary: Returns the calling process.

entries.name: exit
entries.summary:
Sends an exit signal carrying `reason` to `pid`.

`:normal` is the usual shutdown reason; `:kill` cannot be trapped.

entries.name: register
entries.summary: Registers `process` under the atom `name`, so other processes can find it with `whereIs`.

entries.name: whereIs
entries.summary: Returns the process registered under `name`, or `None` when nothing is.

entries.name: Shared
entries.summary:
A named, typed slot that any process can read directly.

State kept in a `serving` process is copied into the caller on every read, which is costly for a large value that every request reads. A `Shared` value is stored once for the whole node (on the BEAM, in `persistent_term`), and reading it copies nothing however large it is.

Writing is the expensive part: replacing a value makes the runtime scan every process for references to the old one. Use it for state that is read constantly and written rarely, such as configuration or a loaded site, not for a counter.

Get a handle with `Process.Shared.named`. The name alone identifies the slot, so two handles with the same name share it. Nothing checks that they agree on the type parameter, so give every handle on one name the same one.

entries.name: named
entries.summary: Returns the handle on the slot called `name`. Nothing is stored or read until `put` or `get`.

entries.name: put
entries.summary:
Stores `value`, replacing whatever the slot held.

This is expensive; see `Process.Shared`.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Returns the stored value, or `None` when nothing has been stored yet.

This is cheap whatever the value's size.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary: Empties the slot and returns what it held.

entries.name: ProcessResult
entries.summary:
The exit status and output of an external command.

`Process.run` returns it inside `Ok` whatever the exit status.

entries.name: Process<X>
entries.summary: Messaging, linking and monitoring a process.

entries.name: send
entries.summary:
Sends `msg` to the process. `msg` must be of the type the process accepts.

Sending never blocks and never fails, even when the process is gone. Monitor the process when you need to know it is still there.

entries.name: sendFrom
entries.summary: Sends the pair `(Process.self, msg)`, so the receiver knows where to reply.

entries.name: link
entries.summary:
Links the calling process to this one, so that if either exits abnormally the other exits too.

Links work in both directions. Use `monitor` to be told about an exit without exiting yourself.

entries.name: unlink
entries.summary: Removes the link between the calling process and this one.

entries.name: monitor
entries.summary:
Starts monitoring this process, and returns the reference that identifies the monitor.

When the monitored process exits, the caller receives a message about it. Unlike `link`, a monitor works in one direction and the caller does not exit with it. Call `demonitor` on the reference to stop.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the process is still running.

The process may exit right after you ask. Monitor it when you need to know when it goes.

entries.name: within
entries.summary:
Returns a handle on the same server with a different call timeout, in milliseconds.

The server and other handles on it are unchanged, so one slow call can be given longer without affecting anyone else.

entries.name: link
entries.summary: Links the calling process to the server. See `Process.link`.

entries.name: unlink
entries.summary: Removes the link between the calling process and the server.

entries.name: monitor
entries.summary: Starts monitoring the server. See `Process.monitor`.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the server is still running.

entries.name: reply
entries.summary:
Sends `value` as the reply to the waiting caller.

A slot that cannot reply at once, because it is waiting on something else, leaves `reply` out of its `Reply` and calls this later.

entries.name: pid
entries.summary: Returns the waiting caller.

entries.name: Task
entries.summary: Running work in another process and collecting the answer.

entries.name: sleep
entries.summary: Suspends the calling process for `duration`. A negative duration counts as zero.

entries.name: start
entries.summary:
Runs `f` in a new process and returns a handle on its result.

The block starts at once. To run several pieces of work at the same time, start all the tasks first and await them afterwards.

entries.name: awaitAll
entries.summary:
Waits for every task in `tasks` and returns their results in the same order.

Each result is a `Result`, as from `await`, so one failed task does not lose the others' results.

entries.name: await

- `:only_crashed`: the crashed child
- `:crashed_and_newer`: it and the children listed after it
- `:all`: every child

The interpreter (`kex -R`) supports only `:only_crashed`, and no nested supervisors.

The parent starts it, and restarts it with all its children when the parent's strategy says so. `restart` takes the same strategies as `Supervisor.start`. It needs the BEAM backend (plain `kex`); `kex -R` does not support it.

entries.name: demonitor
entries.summary: Stops the monitor this reference identifies.

entries.name: Random
entries.summary:
Random numbers, choices and shuffles, for simulations, games and reproducible tests.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Random`. The module functions, such as `Random.integer`, draw from fresh entropy and return the value. For a sequence that can be replayed, start a `Random.Generator` with `Random.seeded`: each of its functions returns `(value, nextGenerator)`, and the next draw is made from `nextGenerator`. Drawing twice from the same generator gives the same value twice.

Invalid arguments, such as a descending range or a probability above 1, end the program with `die`.

None of this is suitable for secrets such as keys or tokens. Use `Random.secureBytes` or `Random.token` for those.

entries.name: Generator
entries.summary:
The state of a reproducible random sequence.

Start one with `Random.seeded` or `Random.fresh`. Each draw returns the value and the advanced generator. The same seed gives the same sequence for the same calls, on the walker and on BEAM.

entries.name: seeded
entries.summary:
Starts a reproducible sequence from `seed`.

Any Integer works, negative or large; it is reduced modulo 2^64.

entries.name: fresh
entries.summary: Starts a generator from fresh entropy, so the sequence differs between runs.

entries.name: integer
entries.summary:
Draws an integer from `range`, both ends included.

The range must be ascending and hold at most 2^64 integers. A range of one integer is allowed and still advances the generator.

entries.name: float
entries.summary:
Draws a float from `range`, which includes its lower bound and excludes its upper one.

Without an argument the range is `0.0..1.0`. The bounds must be finite and strictly ascending.

entries.name: boolean
entries.summary: Draws `true` or `false` with equal probability.

entries.name: chance?
entries.summary:
Draws `true` with the given probability.

Even a probability of 0 or 1 advances the generator.

entries.name: choice
entries.summary:
Picks one element of `items`, each position equally likely.

For an empty list it returns `None` and the generator unchanged.

entries.name: sample
entries.summary:
Picks `count` elements of `items` without replacement, in random order.

Each position is picked at most once, but a value that occurs several times in `items` can occur several times in the result. A `count` larger than the list returns every element, shuffled. A `count` of 0 returns `[]` and leaves the generator unchanged; a negative one ends the program.

entries.name: shuffle
entries.summary:
Returns `items` in random order.

An empty list leaves the generator unchanged.

entries.name: integer

Draws an integer from `range`, both ends included.

The range must be ascending and hold at most 2^64 integers.

entries.name: float
entries.summary:
Draws a float from `range`, which includes its lower bound and excludes its upper one.

The range defaults to `0.0..1.0`. The bounds must be finite and strictly ascending.

entries.name: boolean

entries.name: chance?

entries.name: choice

entries.name: sample

Picks `count` elements of `items` without replacement, in random order.

Each position is picked at most once, but a repeated value can be picked more than once. A `count` larger than the list returns every element.

entries.name: shuffle
entries.summary: Returns `items` in random order.

entries.name: secureBytes
entries.summary:
Returns `count` bytes from the operating system's cryptographically secure generator.

Use it for keys, session tokens and identifiers that must not be guessable; the other functions in this module are not fit for that. The bytes cannot be reproduced, and there is no `Generator` version.

entries.name: token
entries.summary: Returns `bytes` secure random bytes as lowercase hex, a string twice as long as `bytes`.

entries.name: Range
entries.summary:
A span between two bounds, written `(1..10)` or `('a'..'z')`.

Both ends are included. A range holds only its endpoints (and a step), so a large one costs nothing until you enumerate it. Integer and character ranges can be enumerated. A Float range such as `(-1.0..1.0)` is a pair of bounds, useful for `contains?` or random sampling, and cannot be enumerated. A range whose lower end is above its upper end is empty, so `(1..count).each` does nothing when `count` is 0.

```kex
(1..5).items          # => [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
(1..5).sum            # => 15
5.in?(1..10)          # => true
('a'..'e').items      # => ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']
```

To count down or by another step, use `by` or `Integer.downTo`:

```kex
(1..10).by(2).items   # => [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
(10..1).by(-3).items  # => [10, 7, 4, 1]
10.downTo(8).items    # => [10, 9, 8]
(1..4).reverse.items  # => [4, 3, 2, 1]
```

A range of Integers or Chars (a `Discrete` type) is `Enumerable` and `Foldable`, and the list functions below return lists. A Float range has only `contains?`. Use `items` to get the elements as a list.

```kex
(1..10).items.filter(~even?)   # => [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
(1..3).items.each { |n| IO.printLine(n) }
```

entries.name: Discrete
entries.summary:
The element types with a next value, whose ranges can be enumerated: Integer and Char.

A Float range has no next value, so it has `contains?` and none of the traversal functions; `(0.0..1.0).sum` is a type error.

signatures: reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `value` lies between the endpoints, both included.

A range with the default step only compares `value` with the endpoints, so this is cheap for any size of range and works for a `Float` range. A range whose lower end is above its upper end contains nothing. A stepped range contains only the values its step reaches.

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B
entries.summary:
Folds over the range's elements in order.

The `Enumerable` functions are built on it. It builds the list of elements first.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each element in order, for its side effects.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Returns a list of `f` applied to each element, in order.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Returns the sum of the range's elements.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Returns the product of the range's elements.

entries.name: by
entries.summary:
Returns the range counted by `step` from its first endpoint towards its last.

A negative step counts down, and a range whose end lies the other way from its start is empty. The last endpoint is included only when the step lands on it.

A step of 0 is a run-time error. `by` on a `Float` range is a type error.

entries.name: items
entries.summary:
Returns the range's elements as a list.

This builds the whole list, so it costs memory for a very large range.

entries.name: first
entries.summary: Returns the first element, or `None` for an empty range.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns the second element, or `None` when the range is shorter than two.

entries.name: third

entries.summary: Returns every element after the first, as a list.

entries.summary: Returns how many elements the range has.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns how many elements the range has, as `length` does.

entries.name: empty?

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the largest element, or `None` for an empty range.

entries.name: min

entries.name: minBy
entries.summary: Returns the element with the smallest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty range. The first of several tying elements wins.

entries.name: maxBy
entries.summary: Returns the element with the largest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty range. The first of several tying elements wins.

entries.name: sortBy
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list sorted by the key `f` gives each one, smallest key first. The sort is stable: elements with equal keys keep their order.

entries.name: groupBy

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary:
Returns a range of the same elements in the opposite order.

It starts at the last element the step reaches, so `(1..10).by(3).reverse` is `(10..1).by(-3)` and `(1..9).by(3).reverse` is `(7..1).by(-3)`. An empty range stays empty.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list in ascending order, whatever the step.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list, ordered by `comparator`.

entries.name: uniq
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list with duplicates removed. A range has no duplicates, so this is the same as `items`.

entries.name: join
entries.summary: Renders the elements as text, with `separator` between them.

entries.name: at
entries.summary:
Returns the element at index `index`, counting from 0, or `None` when out of range.

The index counts positions, not values: `(10..20).at(0)` is `Just(10)`.

entries.name: get
entries.summary: Returns the element at index `index`, counting from 0, or `None` when out of range. The same as `at`, named to match `List` and `Map`.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` elements as a list.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary: Returns everything after the first `n` elements, as a list.

entries.name: indexOf
entries.summary: Returns the position of `value` in the range, or `None` when it is not in it.

entries.name: zip
entries.summary: Pairs each element with the element at the same position in `other`, stopping at the shorter of the two.

entries.name: partition
entries.summary: Splits the elements into those satisfying `pred` and those that do not.

entries.name: push
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list with `value` added at the end.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns the elements that fail `pred`, as a list.

entries.name: countThrough
entries.summary: `f` applied to each integer from `at` through `last`.

entries.name: countBy
signatures: countBy(at: Integer, last: Integer, step: Integer, f)
