entries.name: Regex
entries.summary:
Regular expressions in PCRE syntax. Bring them into scope with `using Regex`.

There are two ways to write a pattern. The usual one is the tagged literal `` re`...` ``, which is checked when the program is compiled and gives a `Regex` directly.

```kex
using Regex

main do
  let line = "order #4271 shipped"
  IO.printLine(line.matches?(re`#\d+`))                     # => true
  IO.printLine(line.matches(re`#(\d+)`).into { |m| m.get(1) }.or(""))  # => 4271
end
```

The call form `regex(source)` takes a pattern built at run time and returns a `Result`, since the string may not be a valid pattern:

```kex
match regex(userSupplied) do
  Ok(pattern) => IO.printLine(text.matches?(pattern))
  Error(e)    => IO.printError("bad pattern at ${e.position}: ${e.message}")
end
```

The operations are `matches?` (is it there), `matches` (the first match), `scan` (every match), `replace`, `replaceFirst`, `split` and `splitLimit`.

A compiled regular expression.

Create one with a `re` tagged literal or `regex(source)`.

```kex
let digits = re`[0-9]+`
"item 42".matches(digits).into { |m| m.get(0) }   # => Just("42")
```

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Returns the regex written as a `re` literal, which is what interpolation shows.

entries.name: RegexError
entries.summary:
A pattern that failed to compile.

`position` counts characters, not bytes, from the start of the pattern.

```kex
regex("(")
# => Error(Regex.RegexError { message: "missing closing parenthesis",
#                             position: 1, source: "(" })
```

entries.name: regex
entries.summary:
Compiles `source` into a `Regex`.

Use it for a pattern built at run time, such as one read from a config file or typed by a user. For a pattern written in the source, the tag form `` regex`\d+` `` is checked at compile time and returns a `Regex` directly.

entries.name: withOptions
signatures: withOptions(source: String, options: {Atom: Bool}) -> Result<Regex, RegexError>
entries.summary:
Compiles `source` with matching options, like Ruby's `Regexp.new(source, options)`.

The options are `ignoreCase` (`/i`), `multiline` (`^` and `$` match at every line), `dotAll` (`.` also matches a newline) and `extended` (whitespace and `#` comments in the pattern are ignored). An option set to `false` is the same as leaving it out, and an unknown one is a `RegexError` at position 0.

The options are added to the pattern as an inline `(?imsx)` prefix, so the resulting `source` shows them. Positions in a compile error still count from the start of `source` as you passed it.

entries.name: validateRegex
entries.summary:
Checks a `regex` tagged literal at compile time.

The compiler finds it by the `validate<Tag>` naming convention described in `TaggedValidation`. An invalid literal such as `` regex`(` `` is a compile error, with the caret at the offset where the pattern went wrong.

entries.name: re
entries.summary:
A short name for `regex`, in both its call and tag forms.

It behaves exactly like `regex`. Most code uses it as a tag, where the shorter name reads better.

entries.name: validateRe
entries.summary: Checks an `re` tagged literal at compile time, as `validateRegex` does.

entries.name: quote
entries.summary:
Returns `s` with every regex metacharacter escaped, as a pattern that matches `s` literally.

Use it to search for text that may contain pattern syntax, such as a search term typed by a user or a file name. Each character is escaped on its own, so a `\E` in `s` cannot end the quoting early as it would inside `\Q...\E`.

entries.name: Match
entries.summary:
A successful match, and the groups it captured.

Read groups with `get`, by number (`0` is the whole match) or by name (`:year`).

A group that took no part in the match is missing, so `get` returns `None`. A group that matched the empty string returns `Just("")`.

entries.name: Match
signatures: get(key: Atom | Integer, default: String) -> String

entries.name: get
signatures: get(key: Atom | Integer, default: String) -> String
entries.summary:
Returns the text captured by a group, by number or by name.

Group `0` is the whole match; `1` is the first parenthesised group. A named group `(?<year>...)` is read with the atom `:year`. A group that took no part in the match returns `None`.

entries.name: matches
entries.summary:
Finds the first occurrence of `re` in `s` and returns what it matched.

The pattern may match anywhere in the string; anchor it with `^...$` to match the whole string. Returns `None` when the pattern does not occur.

entries.name: matches?
entries.summary:
Returns whether `re` occurs anywhere in `s`.

Like `matches`, the pattern is not anchored.

entries.name: scan
entries.summary:
Returns every match of `re` in `s`, left to right.

The result is a list of `Match` whether or not the pattern has groups, so adding a group does not change its type. An empty list means nothing matched.

entries.name: replace
signatures: replace(s: String, re: Regex, replacement: (String | (Match) -> String)) -> String
entries.summary:
Returns `s` with every match of `re` replaced, like Ruby's `gsub`.

The replacement is a `String`, inserted as it is (`$1` and `\1` have no special meaning), or a block that gets the `Match` and returns the text. Use the block to build the replacement from the captured groups.

entries.name: replaceFirst
signatures: replaceFirst(s: String, re: Regex, replacement: (String | (Match) -> String)) -> String
entries.summary:
Returns `s` with only the first match of `re` replaced, like Ruby's `sub`.

The replacement works as for `replace`.

entries.name: splitLimit
signatures: splitLimit(s: String, re: Regex, limit: Integer) -> [String]
entries.summary:
Splits `s` on `re`, with a limit on the fields.

A positive `limit` is the most fields to return, and the last one holds the rest of the string unsplit. A negative `limit` keeps trailing empty fields, which are dropped otherwise.

Without a limit, use `s.split(re)`. It follows Ruby: trailing empty fields are dropped, leading ones kept, and the text of capture groups is included between the fields.

entries.name: Stream
entries.summary:
A lazy, potentially infinite sequence.

A stream holds the rule for producing its elements, so it can be infinite. Elements are computed only when you ask for them with `take`.

```kex
let naturals = Stream.from(0) { |n| n + 1 }
naturals.take(5)                              # => [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
naturals.map { |n| n * n }.take(4)            # => [0, 1, 4, 9]
naturals.filter { |n| n.even? }.take(3)       # => [0, 2, 4]
```

`map`, `filter` and `drop` return another stream, so a whole pipeline stays lazy until `take` turns it into a list.

Streams suit generated sequences that you may read more than once. A file or socket can only be read once, so functions that read them return a `Feed`. A feed's `toStream` gives a stream that can be replayed, at the cost of keeping every value read so far, so use it only for small inputs.

entries.name: Stream
entries.summary: Constructors for `Stream`.

entries.name: from
entries.summary:
Builds an infinite stream from a first element and a step function.

The stream is `start`, then `step(start)`, then `step(step(start))`, and so on. Nothing is computed until you take from it.

entries.name: empty
entries.summary: Returns the stream with no elements.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` elements as a list, computing the stream up to that point. It is how a lazy pipeline ends.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream that skips the first `n` elements.

The result is still lazy. Follow it with `take` to get a window from the middle.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream with `f` applied to each element.

`f` is not called until elements are taken, and then only for those that are.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream with only the elements `pred` accepts.

Taking `n` filtered elements may mean computing many more elements of the original stream. If `pred` rarely holds, `take` runs for a long time; if it never holds, `take` never returns.

entries.name: each
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to every element, for its side effects.

It only finishes on a stream that ends, such as a file's lines converted with `Feed.toStream`. On an infinite stream from `Stream.from` it never returns, so bound it with `take` first.

entries.name: toFeed
entries.summary:
Returns a `Feed` that walks this stream once.

A stream keeps every element computed from it for as long as the stream is in scope. A feed lets each element go once it has been read, so use `toFeed` to walk a long stream in constant memory.

entries.name: String
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> Char -> A)) -> A
identifierWords(chars: [Char], previous: Char?, current: String, words: [String]) -> [String]
entries.summary:
Text. A `String` is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters; functions that transform text return a new string.

A `String` is its own type, not a list of characters. It is `Enumerable`, so `each`, `reduce` and `find` walk it one `Char` at a time. Sequence functions return whichever type is more useful: `take`, `drop` and `sort` return a `String`, while `first` and `last` return a `Char`. Use `chars` to get a `[Char]`.

```kex
let line = "  Hello, World  "
line.trim.lowerCase.split(", ")   # => ["hello", "world"]
line.trim.take(5)                 # => "Hello"
line.trim.chars.count(~upper?)    # => 2
```

Strings interpolate with `${...}`:

```kex
let name = "Ada"
"hello, ${name}"                  # => "hello, Ada"
```

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> Char -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Folds the string from the left, one `Char` at a time.

`String`'s other `Enumerable` functions, such as `map`, `find` and `any?`, are built on this one. Use it directly to accumulate something that is neither a string nor a list.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each character, for its side effects.

entries.name: mapChars
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to every character and joins the results into a `String`.

`map`, from `Enumerable`, returns a list, since its function may return something other than a `Char`. Use `mapChars` when you want a string back.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary: Returns the characters satisfying `pred`, as a `String`.

entries.name: uniq
entries.summary: Returns the string with repeated characters removed, keeping the first occurrence of each.

entries.name: first
entries.summary:
A String is its own type, not a [Char], so the sequence functions below are declared here instead of coming from List: `take`/`drop`/`sort` return a String, `first`/`last` a Char. The List intrinsics they call understand the String representation.

Returns the first character, or `None` when the string is empty.

entries.name: last
entries.summary: Returns the last character, or `None` when the string is empty.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Returns the character at index `i`, counting from 0.

A negative index counts back from the end, so `-1` is the last character. An index past either end returns `None`.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` characters, or the whole string when it is shorter than `n`.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary: Returns everything after the first `n` characters, so +s.take(n) + s.drop(n)+ is `s`.

entries.name: slice
entries.summary:
Returns the substring of `length` characters starting at index `start`, counting from 0.

Indices count characters, not bytes. Out-of-range values are clamped, as in `take` and `drop`: a start past the end or a negative length returns `""`, and a length running past the end stops there. A negative start counts back from the end, as in Ruby, so `-1` is the last character; a start that is still before the beginning returns `""`.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns the characters that do not satisfy `pred`, as a `String`.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the characters in ascending codepoint order.

entries.name: indexOf
entries.summary: Returns the index of the first occurrence of `c`, or `None` when the character does not appear.

entries.name: findIndex
entries.summary: Returns the index of the first character satisfying `pred`, or `None`. Use `indexOf` to search for a known character.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.summary: Returns the leading characters that satisfy `pred`, stopping at the first that does not.

entries.name: dropWhile
entries.summary: Drops the leading characters that satisfy `pred` and returns the rest.

entries.name: zip
entries.summary: Pairs each character with the element at the same index in `other`, stopping at the shorter of the two.

entries.name: partition
entries.summary: Splits the string in two: the characters satisfying `pred`, then those that do not.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of characters (codepoints), not bytes. `byteSize` gives the encoded length, and `graphemeCount` the characters a reader sees.

entries.name: occurrences
entries.summary: Returns how many times `sub` occurs, counting non-overlapping matches from the left. An empty `sub` occurs 0 times. Ruby writes this `scan(sub).size`; Kex's `count` with a predicate counts characters.

entries.name: length
entries.summary: Returns the number of characters. The same as `count`.

entries.name: graphemeCount
entries.summary:
Returns the number of user-perceived characters, counted as extended grapheme clusters (Unicode UAX #29).

`count` counts codepoints. The two agree for most text, but differ for a letter followed by a combining mark, an emoji made of several codepoints, and `"\r\n"`, which is one cluster of two codepoints. Use `graphemeCount` when the question is how many characters a person sees, for example when sizing text for display.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the string has no characters.

A string of spaces is not empty; use `blank?` from `Blankable` when whitespace should not count.

entries.name: enclose
entries.summary: Returns the string with `wrapper` added at both ends.

entries.name: at
entries.summary: Returns the character at index `i`, counting from 0, or `None` when the index is out of range. A negative index counts from the end. The same as `get(i)`.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns the second character, or `None` when the string is shorter than two characters.

entries.name: third
entries.summary: Returns the third character, or `None` when the string is shorter than three characters.

entries.name: rest
entries.summary: Returns everything after the first character, or `""` for the empty string.

entries.name: chars
entries.summary:
Returns the string's characters as a list.

Use it to reach `List` functions that `String` lacks, and `join("")` to get back to a string.

entries.name: bytes
entries.summary:
Returns the string's UTF-8 encoding, one `Byte` per byte.

`chars` and `bytes` differ outside ASCII: `"é"` is one `Char` and two bytes. Use `bytes` when the encoded form matters, as in a network frame or a size limit. `String.fromBytes` is the inverse.

entries.name: byteSize
entries.summary:
Returns the length of the string's UTF-8 encoding in bytes.

It gives the same number as `bytes.count` without building a list of every byte, which matters for large payloads.

entries.name: byteAt
entries.summary:
Returns the byte at a UTF-8 offset, or `None` when the offset is out of range.

The offset indexes the encoding, so inside a multi-byte character it returns one of that character's bytes. Use `at` to index characters.

entries.name: bytePart
entries.summary:
Returns the bytes from `offset` to +offset + count+ of the UTF-8 encoding, as a `String`.

Out-of-range values are clamped, as in `take` and `drop`. Cutting inside a character leaves partial UTF-8 in the result, so slice only at offsets you know are character boundaries.

entries.name: split
entries.summary:
Splits the string into its individual characters, as one-character strings.

Use `chars` to get `Char` values.

entries.name: split
entries.summary:
Splits the string on every occurrence of `sep`, which may be a literal string or a `Regex`.

Separators at the ends produce empty parts, so splitting `",a,"` on `","` gives three parts.

entries.name: lines
entries.summary:
Splits the string into lines on `\n`.

A single trailing newline is dropped, so a file that ends in one gives no final empty line. A Windows `\r\n` counts as one line ending, so no line keeps a stray `\r`. `FS.File.readLines`, `FileHandle.getLine` and file feeds split lines the same way.

entries.name: indentRest
entries.summary:
Indents every line but the first by `prefix`.

Use it to splice a multi-line value into an indented `${...}` hole, where the text before the hole already indents the first line. Blank lines stay blank, and a single trailing newline is dropped, as `lines` does.

entries.name: replace
entries.summary:
Replaces every literal occurrence of `pattern` with `replacement`.

The pattern is matched literally, not as a regular expression. An empty pattern matches at every character boundary, including both ends.

entries.name: replaceFirst
entries.summary: Replaces only the first literal occurrence of `pattern`. Ruby calls this `sub`, and `replace` is its `gsub`.

entries.name: substitute
entries.summary:
Replaces every occurrence of each key of `replacements` with its value.

Keys are matched literally, with no placeholder syntax, so `$NAME$`, `__NAME__` and `{{name}}` all work. `$NAME$` is the usual convention. A placeholder cannot be written `${name}` in a string literal, because that is interpolation and is filled in before `substitute` runs.

Substitutions run in the map's key order, each on the result of the last, so a later key can rewrite text that an earlier value put in.

entries.name: trim
entries.summary: Removes leading and trailing whitespace, leaving whitespace inside the string alone.

entries.name: trimStart
entries.summary: Removes leading whitespace only. Ruby calls this `lstrip`.

entries.name: trimEnd
entries.summary: Removes trailing whitespace only. Ruby calls this `rstrip`.

entries.name: removePrefix
entries.summary: Removes `prefix` from the start of the string if it is there. Ruby calls this `delete_prefix`.

entries.name: removeSuffix
entries.summary: Removes `suffix` from the end of the string if it is there. Ruby calls this `delete_suffix`.

entries.name: padLeft
entries.summary: Pads the string on the left with spaces until it is `width` characters long. A string already that long is returned unchanged. Ruby calls this `rjust`.

entries.name: padRight
entries.summary: Pads the string on the right with spaces until it is `width` characters long. Ruby calls this `ljust`.

entries.name: center
entries.summary: Centers the string in a field of `width` characters, padding both sides with spaces. When the padding cannot split evenly, the extra character goes on the right, as Ruby's `center` does.

entries.name: upperCase
entries.summary: Returns the string with every character converted to upper case.

entries.name: lowerCase
entries.summary: Returns the string with every character converted to lower case.

entries.name: capitalize
entries.summary:
Returns the string with its first character upper-cased and the rest LOWER-cased.

As in Ruby, `"hELLO"` becomes `"Hello"`. It is handy in a `compiled do` block for turning a lower-case word into the upper-case name that `type %name` requires.

entries.name: snakeCase
entries.summary:
Returns the identifier in `snake_case`: its words lower-cased and joined with underscores.

Words are separated by `_`, `-` and spaces, and by case: a capital after a lower-case letter or digit starts a word (`userId`), and so does the last capital of a run followed by a lower-case letter (`HTTPServer` is `HTTP`, `Server`). Anything else stays in its word, so `empty?` keeps its `?`.

entries.name: kebabCase
entries.summary: Returns the identifier in `kebab-case`: its words lower-cased and joined with hyphens. Words are found as `snakeCase` finds them.

entries.name: camelCase
entries.summary: Returns the identifier in `camelCase`: its first word lower-cased and the rest capitalized, with nothing between them. Words are found as `snakeCase` finds them.

entries.name: pascalCase
entries.summary: Returns the identifier in `PascalCase`: every word capitalized, with nothing between them. Words are found as `snakeCase` finds them.

entries.name: filler
entries.summary: `pad` repeated and cut to exactly `width` characters: the filler the padding functions put beside the string. Nothing for a width of 0 or less, or for an empty `pad`.

entries.name: identifierWords
signatures: identifierWords(chars: [Char], previous: Char?, current: String, words: [String]) -> [String]
entries.summary: The words of an identifier, read one character at a time: `previous` is the character before `chars`, `current` the word being read. `words` is kept newest first, since on BEAM `[w | words]` is cheap and `words + [w]` copies them all, and is reversed once at the end.

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary: Returns the string with its characters in reverse order.

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `sub` appears anywhere in the string.

The search is literal and case-sensitive. Lower-case both sides to ignore case, or use `Regex` to search for a pattern.

entries.name: startsWith?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the string begins with `prefix`.

entries.name: endsWith?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the string ends with `suffix`.

entries.name: Char
entries.summary:
A single Unicode character.

Character literals use single quotes (`'a'`), and `'a'` is a different type from the one-character string `"a"`. The predicates `digit?`, `alpha?`, `space?` and the rest classify a character; `codepoint` and `String.fromCodepoint` convert to and from Unicode values.

```kex
"hello world".chars.count(~alpha?)   # => 10
'a'.upperCase                        # => 'A'
'a'.string                           # => "a"
```

entries.name: string
entries.summary:
Returns this character as a one-character `String`.

`to(String)` also works but returns `String?`, like every `to` conversion; `string` cannot fail, so it returns the `String` directly.

entries.name: upperCase
entries.summary:
Returns the upper-case form of this character, still as a `Char`.

Characters with no upper-case form (digits, punctuation) are returned unchanged.

entries.name: lowerCase
entries.summary:
Returns the lower-case form of this character, still as a `Char`.

Characters with no lower-case form are returned unchanged.

entries.name: digit?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character is a decimal digit, `'0'` through `'9'`.

entries.name: alpha?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character is a Unicode letter.

entries.name: letter?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character is a Unicode letter. The same as `alpha?`.

entries.name: upper?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the character is upper case.

Characters without case, such as digits and punctuation, return `false`.

entries.name: lower?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character is lower case.

entries.name: space?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character is Unicode whitespace, such as a space, tab, newline or no-break space.

entries.name: codepoint
entries.summary:
Returns the character's Unicode codepoint.

`String.fromCodepoint` is the inverse.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the character falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: String
entries.summary: Builds `String` values from a Unicode codepoint or from UTF-8 bytes.

entries.name: fromCodepoint
entries.summary:
Builds a one-character string from a Unicode codepoint.

Returns `None` for a surrogate or a value outside the Unicode range. `Char.codepoint` is the inverse.

entries.name: fromBytes
entries.summary:
Rebuilds a string from its UTF-8 bytes: the inverse of `bytes`.

Returns `None` for a value outside 0..255 or for malformed UTF-8; invalid bytes are never turned into replacement characters.

entries.name: Tuple
entries.summary:
A fixed-size group of values, written `(a, b)`. A tuple's size and the type of each position are part of its type, and `List` functions do not apply to it: destructure it, match on it, or convert it with `items`.

```kex
let (name, age) = ("Ada", 36)
[1, 2, 3].partition { |n| n.even? }   # => ([2], [1, 3])
```

entries.name: items
entries.summary:
Returns the tuple's elements as a list.

The list is typed `[Any]`, so the type of each position is lost. When you know the shape, destructuring (`let (a, b) = pair`) is usually clearer.

entries.name: System
entries.summary:
Exiting the program, and finding out what platform it runs on.

```kex
System.OS          # => :macos
System.posix?      # => true
System.exit(1)     # ends the program with status 1
```

entries.name: OperatingSystem
entries.summary:
The operating system families a program can run on.

A platform Kex does not recognise is `:unknown`. The set is closed, so a `match` over it can be exhaustive.

entries.name: exit
entries.summary:
Ends the process at once with exit status `code`.

The status goes to whatever started the program: 0 means success, and anything else means failure. Nothing after the call runs, and nothing is cleaned up, so close what needs closing first.

entries.name: OS
entries.summary:
The operating system family this program is running on.

For a single yes-or-no question, `macOS?`, `linux?`, `windows?` and `posix?` read better. Use `OS` to branch several ways.

entries.name: BITWIDTH
entries.summary: The machine's pointer width in bits: 64 on current hardware, 32 on some small targets.

entries.name: macOS?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when running on macOS.

entries.name: linux?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when running on Linux.

entries.name: windows?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when running on Windows.

entries.name: posix?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the platform follows POSIX conventions for paths and shells.

That is every supported platform except Windows and WebAssembly. An unknown platform is not assumed to be POSIX.

entries.name: die
entries.summary:
Ends the program with a fatal error message.

`message` goes to stderr after a `"fatal: "` prefix, and the exit status is 1. `die` aborts the program; `trying` and `rescue` cannot catch it. Use it where the program has no way to continue, such as a bad argument to `Random.sample`.

Its result type is `Never`, so a branch that dies takes the type of the other branch: `if b == 0 then die("divide by zero") else a end` is an `Integer`.

`die` is declared at the top level, like `assert`, so it is always in scope.

entries.name: TaggedValidation
signatures: fatalBetween(start: Integer, finish: Integer, message: String) -> Issue
warnBetween(start: Integer, finish: Integer, message: String) -> Issue
entries.summary:
Diagnostics that compile-time validators return for tagged literals.

A tagged literal (`` re`\d+` ``, `` sql`SELECT ...` ``) can be checked when the program is compiled. The compiler looks the checker up by name: tag `foo` is checked by a function `validateFoo` that takes the literal's text and returns a list of `Issue` values. An empty list means the literal is fine.

```kex
let validateHex(source: String) -> [TaggedValidation.Issue] do
  match source.chars.findIndex { |c| !c.digit? && !c.in?('a'..'f') } do
    Just(offset) => [TaggedValidation.fatalAt(offset, "not a hex digit")]
    None         => []
  end
end
```

A `Fatal` issue fails the build with its message and puts the caret at its offset. A `Warn` issue is reported and the build goes on.

Offsets count bytes from zero, from the start of the literal body after escapes are processed.

entries.name: ByteSpan
entries.summary:
Where in the literal an issue applies: one offset, or a range.

Both count bytes into the literal body from zero.

entries.name: Issue
entries.summary:
One diagnostic about a tagged literal.

`Fatal` fails the build and `Warn` is reported while the build goes on. An issue about the whole literal has `None` for its span.

entries.name: fatal
entries.summary: Returns a fatal issue about the whole literal, with no position.

entries.name: fatalAt
entries.summary:
Returns a fatal issue at one offset in the literal.

The compiler's error puts its caret at `offset`, so pass the position your checker reported.

entries.name: fatalBetween
signatures: fatalBetween(start: Integer, finish: Integer, message: String) -> Issue
entries.summary: Returns a fatal issue covering a range of the literal.

entries.name: warn
entries.summary: Returns a warning about the whole literal. The build goes on.

entries.name: warnAt
entries.summary: Returns a warning at one offset in the literal.

entries.name: warnBetween
signatures: warnBetween(start: Integer, finish: Integer, message: String) -> Issue
entries.summary: Returns a warning covering a range of the literal.

entries.name: Template
signatures: renderParsed(parsed: Parsed, context: {String: String}) -> Result<String, TemplateError>
render(source: String, context: {String: String}) -> Result<String, TemplateError>
entries.summary:
ERB-style templates: scanning template text into nodes, and filling simple templates at run time.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Template`.

`Template.scan` turns template text into its frontmatter and a flat list of +Node+s: plain text and the four kinds of `<% %>` region. It does not run anything or parse Kex; the text inside a tag is kept as written. `Template.render` fills a template that only substitutes values, from a map. A template with Kex control flow is compiled instead, with `Template.html(Kex.embed(path))` or `Template.text(Kex.embed(path))`.

```kex
using Template

let source = "---\ntitle: Welcome\nparams: [name, library: Bool]\n---\nHi <%= name %>!"
let parsed = Template.scan(source).try
parsed.frontmatter.get("title")    # => Just(Scalar("Welcome"))
parsed.parameters.map { |p| (p.name, p.type) }
# => [("name", ""), ("library", "Bool")]
parsed.nodes                       # => [Text("Hi "), Interpolate("name"), Text("!")]
```

A template file's name puts the extension of what it produces before `.ket`, such as `README.md.ket` or `profile.html.ket`, so an editor can highlight it:

```kex
---
params: [name, library: Bool, dependencies: [Dependency]]
---
# <%= name %>

<% if library %>
A Kex library.
<% else %>
A Kex application.
<% end %>

<% dependencies.map do |dep| %>
- `<%= dep.name %>` ~> <%= dep.version %>
<% end %>
```

## Syntax

```kex
<%= expr %>     inserts the value, HTML-escaped by Template.html and
                Template.render
<%== expr %>    inserts the value without escaping
<% ... %>       Kex control code: if and match arms, block bodies, let
<%# ... %>      a comment, which produces nothing
<%- ... -%>     trims the indentation before the tag and the newline
                after it (see Whitespace below)
<%%             a literal <%, for a template that writes ERB itself
```

## Layouts

A layout is a template that takes the page as a block. The two templates do not refer to each other; the Kex code that calls them puts them together. Insert the block's result with `<%== %>`, since it is already rendered, and already escaped if it came from `Template.html`.

```kex
---
params: [title: String, content: Block<String>]
---
<title><%= title %></title>
<main><%== content() %></main>

let frame = Template.html(Kex.embed("views/layouts/auth.html.ket"))
let form = Template.html(Kex.embed("views/signin.html.ket"))

let signin(email: String) -> String = frame("Sign in") { form(email) }
```

## Whitespace

A `<% %>` or `<%# %>` tag that is alone on its line, with only whitespace around it, removes the whole line from the output, its indentation and newline included. So the template reads the way its output does:

```kex
<% if dependencies.count > 0 %>
## Dependencies
<% end %>

# => "## Dependencies\n", with no blank lines where the tags were
```

The `<%-` and `-%>` markers are for a tag that shares its line with other content, where only the author knows what should be trimmed:

```kex
Total: <%= total %> <%- if pending > 0 %>(<%= pending %> pending)<% end %>
```

An interpolation is never trimmed, even alone on its line. It stands for content, so the whitespace around it is content too:

```kex
<%= greeting %>
<%= name %>

# => "Hi\nAda\n", with both newlines kept
```

## Frontmatter

A template may start with a `---` line, then `key: value` lines, then a closing `---` line before the body. The keys are for whatever reads the template, such as a title or a list of tags, and the scanner reads every key the same way. A value is a plain string or a `[a, b, c]` list.

```kex
---
title: Release notes
tags: [changelog, public]
---
# <%= title %>
```

By convention, a template declares its parameters under `params`, as a list of names, each with an optional `: Type`:

```kex
---
params: [name, library: Bool, dependencies: [Dependency]]
---
# <%= name %>
```

`Parsed.parameters` reads that list and splits each entry at its first colon into a `TemplateParam`. The type stays text: `[Dependency]` is the string `"[Dependency]"`, not a resolved Kex type.

entries.name: Node
entries.summary:
One piece of a scanned template: plain text, or one kind of tag with the text inside it.

The text inside a tag is the Kex source between the delimiters, with the surrounding whitespace trimmed. It is not parsed.

entries.name: Tag
entries.summary: A frontmatter value: a plain string, or a `[a, b, c]` list.

entries.name: TemplateError
entries.summary:
The reason a template could not be scanned or rendered.

`UnterminatedTag` carries the character position of the tag that is not closed. `MalformedFrontmatterLine` carries the offending line. `UndefinedVariable` and `UnsupportedControl` come from `Template.render` and `Template.renderParsed`, and carry the tag's text.

entries.name: TemplateParam
entries.summary:
One entry of a `params: [...]` frontmatter list: a name and its type.

`type` is the text after the colon, or `""` for a bare name. It is not resolved to a Kex type.

entries.name: TagScan
entries.summary:
One scanned `<% ... %>` tag and the whitespace trims its delimiters ask for. Used inside the scanner only.

It is declared outside `private do` because a record nested there loses its field names on BEAM.

entries.name: Parsed
entries.summary: A scanned template: its frontmatter, and its body as a list of nodes.

entries.name: parameters
entries.summary:
Returns the parameters declared under the template's `params` key, in the order written.

Returns `[]` when there is no `params` key, or when its value is not a list.

entries.name: scan
entries.summary: Scans template text into its frontmatter and nodes.

entries.name: escapeHtml
entries.summary:
Escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, double quotes and single quotes, so the text is safe in HTML content and in quoted attribute values.

`Template.html` escapes `<%= %>` tags this way. It does not make text safe inside a URL, a script or a style sheet.

entries.name: renderParsed
signatures: renderParsed(parsed: Parsed, context: {String: String}) -> Result<String, TemplateError>
entries.summary:
Fills a scanned template with the values in `context`.

`<%= %>` inserts the value HTML-escaped, and `<%== %>` inserts it as is. Only substitution is supported: a `<% ... %>` control tag gives an `UnsupportedControl` error. For templates with control flow, use `Template.html` or `Template.text`, which compile the template.

Each tag's trimmed text is looked up as a key, whole. `<%= dep.name %>` reads the `"dep.name"` key; it does not read a field of a value under `"dep"`.

entries.name: render
signatures: render(source: String, context: {String: String}) -> Result<String, TemplateError>
entries.summary: Scans `source` and fills it with the values in `context`, as `Template.renderParsed` does.

entries.name: describe
signatures: describe(label: String, block: Block<Result<Void, Any>>) -> Void
entries.summary:
Groups related test cases under a label and runs them.

The block runs at once. `describe` blocks nest, and the output is indented to match.

entries.name: it
signatures: it(label: String, block: Block<Result<Void, Any>>) -> Void
entries.summary:
Defines a single test case and runs it.

A failed assertion, or anything else that fails inside the block, marks the test failed and the rest of the suite carries on. A `.try` that fails in the block fails the test too, so the body needs no `Ok` or `rescue`.

entries.name: before
entries.summary:
Registers setup to run before the current group's tests.

`before { ... }` and `before(:each) { ... }` run before every test in the group; `before(:all) { ... }` runs once before the group's first test, following RSpec's scope convention.

entries.name: after
entries.summary:
Registers cleanup to run after the current group's tests.

Runs after every test, whether it passed or failed. Inner groups' hooks run before outer ones.

entries.name: assert
entries.summary:
Fails the enclosing `it` when `value` is `false`.

The `Assert` functions are built on it. Prefer them where one fits, since their failure message shows the values involved.

entries.name: Assert
entries.summary:
Assertions whose failure message shows what was expected and what arrived. They are written in Kex on top of `assert`.

```kex
Assert.equal("hi".upperCase, "HI")
Assert.some(users.first)
Assert.ok(Integer.parse("42"))
```

entries.name: equal
entries.summary:
Fails unless `actual` equals `expected`, reporting both.

Use it by default for comparisons: unlike `assert(a == b)`, a failure shows both values.

entries.name: notEqual
entries.summary: Fails when `actual` equals `expected`.

entries.name: truthy
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is truthy: anything except `false` and `None`.

entries.name: falsy
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is falsy: `false`, `None` or `()`.

entries.name: some
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is a `Just`.

entries.name: none
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is `None`.

entries.name: ok
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is an `Ok`.

entries.name: error
entries.summary: Fails unless `value` is an `Error`.

entries.name: TimeError
entries.summary: The error for a date or time field out of range, or for text that is not a date or time.

entries.name: Time
entries.summary:
A time of day, with no date and no zone.

```kex
let t = Time.of(14, 3, 0).try
t.iso                  # => "14:03:00"
(t + 2.hour).iso       # => "16:03:00"
```

Arithmetic wraps around midnight, since there is no date to carry into. Use `DateTime` when crossing into the next day matters.

entries.name: Time
signatures: of(hour: Integer, minute: Integer, second: Integer, nanosecond: Integer) -> Result<Time, TimeError>
daysInMonth(year: Integer, month: Integer) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
daysFromCivil(year: Integer, month: Integer, day: Integer) -> Integer
digitsIn(fragment: String, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
fixedDigitsIn(fragment: String, width: Integer, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
parseFraction(text: String, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
entries.summary: Functions for building times of day, the clock capability, and the calendar arithmetic the other time types use.

entries.name: of
signatures: of(hour: Integer, minute: Integer, second: Integer, nanosecond: Integer) -> Result<Time, TimeError>
entries.summary:
Builds a time of day, checking every field.

A second of 60 is rejected, since leap seconds are not modeled.

entries.name: midnight
entries.summary: Returns midnight, 00:00:00.

entries.name: fromSecondsSinceMidnight
entries.summary:
The one-argument form is declared first: the interpreter resolves an overloaded module function to its last definition regardless of arity, so a delegating overload placed second would call itself.

Builds a time of day from a number of seconds since midnight.

The count wraps around the day, so 86400 is midnight again and -1 is 23:59:59. Unlike `Time.of`, it cannot fail.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an ISO 8601 time of day: `14:03`, `14:03:00` or `14:03:00.123456789`.

Each field must have two digits. Anything else is an `InvalidFormat` error, and an out-of-range field is `InvalidTime`.

entries.name: now
entries.summary:
Returns the current time of day in this machine's zone.

It reads `Time.Clock`, so a test can fix it by replacing that capability.

entries.name: utcNow
entries.summary: Returns the current time of day in UTC.

entries.name: parseOffset
entries.summary:
Parses an ISO 8601 zone designator, such as `Z`, `02:00` or -05:30, into an offset from UTC.

`Z` and the empty string both mean UTC. Otherwise the text must be a sign and two-digit hours and minutes, separated by a colon.

entries.name: Time.Clock
entries.summary:
The clock, which every function that needs the current instant reads.

`Time.now`, `Date.today` and `DateTime.utcNow` all read it, so replacing it changes what all of them see. The replacement applies to a block: it reaches every call made inside the block and every process started there, it can be nested, and it ends with the block. That makes code that calls `Date.today()` testable:

```kex
with Time.Clock = Mock.Clock { at: DateTime.parse("2026-07-30T14:03:00Z").try } do
  Date.today().iso   # always "2026-07-30"
end
```

`now` is its only function. The instant it returns carries the local offset, so it also says which zone the machine is in. `Mock.Clock` is a ready-made replacement, and any record that implements `now` can be one.

entries.name: now
entries.summary: Returns the current instant, with this machine's current UTC offset.

entries.name: momentAt
entries.summary:
Returns the instant `nanos` nanoseconds after the Unix epoch, with the offset this machine's zone has at that instant.

It is `foul` because the machine's zone is outside the program.

entries.name: nanosOf
entries.summary:
A plain function, not a DateTime function: on BEAM a function named epochNanos would share its name with the DateTime.epochNanos() module function, and the arity-0 one would win, reading the host clock instead of moment.

Returns the number of nanoseconds from the Unix epoch to `moment`.

entries.name: leapYear?
entries.summary:
The functions below are public because the make blocks at file level call them, and they are useful on their own too.

Returns `true` when `year` is a leap year in the proleptic Gregorian calendar.

entries.name: daysInMonth
signatures: daysInMonth(year: Integer, month: Integer) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
entries.summary:
Returns the number of days in a month of a given year.

The year comes first, as in `Date.of(year, month, day)`. A month outside 1 through 12 gives `Error(InvalidDate(year, month, 1))`.

entries.name: daysInValidMonth
entries.summary:
Returns the number of days in a month that is known to be 1 through 12.

Use `daysInMonth` for a month from outside the program.

entries.name: daysFromCivil
signatures: daysFromCivil(year: Integer, month: Integer, day: Integer) -> Integer
entries.summary:
Returns the number of days from 1970-01-01 to a calendar date, negative for earlier dates.

It uses Howard Hinnant's algorithms, which are exact across the whole proleptic Gregorian calendar.

entries.name: civilFromDays
entries.summary: Returns the date a number of days after 1970-01-01; the inverse of `daysFromCivil`.

entries.name: weekdayFromEpochDay
entries.summary: Returns the weekday of the date a number of days after 1970-01-01.

entries.name: weekdayNumber
entries.summary:
Returns the ISO number of a weekday: 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday.

`weekday.number` reads better.

entries.name: weekdayName
entries.summary:
Returns the English name of a weekday.

`weekday.name` reads better.

entries.name: number
entries.summary: Returns the weekday's ISO number: 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday.

entries.name: name
entries.summary: Returns the weekday's English name.

entries.name: weekend?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for Saturday and Sunday.

entries.name: errorMessage
entries.summary:
A plain function, not an Errorable implementation: a message function here would share BEAM's dispatcher with the message field of PatternError and break it (spec/record_field_method_collision.kex).

Returns a `TimeError` as a sentence for a person to read.

entries.name: formatFraction
entries.summary: Formats a fraction of a second for ISO 8601 output: 3, 6 or 9 digits, whichever is the shortest that loses nothing, with a leading `.`. A fraction of 0 gives `""`, so `14:03:00` has no fraction.

entries.name: formatOffset
entries.summary: Formats an offset from UTC as ISO 8601 `±HH:MM`, or `Z` for UTC.

entries.name: truncatedBy
entries.summary:
Returns how many whole +unit+s fit in `seconds`.

Both are rounded to the nanosecond first, since a `Duration` holds Float seconds: 7 nanoseconds is 7e-9 seconds, and dividing that by 1e-9 gives 6.999..., which would truncate to 6.

entries.name: padTo
entries.summary: Pads `value` with leading zeros to `width` digits. A wider value is left as it is, not cut.

entries.name: padYear
entries.summary: Formats a year with at least four digits. ISO 8601 sets no width for other years, so they are written as they are.

entries.name: digitsIn
signatures: digitsIn(fragment: String, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
entries.summary: Reads `fragment` as ASCII digits. On failure, the error names `whole`, the full input: `Time.parse("2:03 pm")` should report "2:03 pm", not "03 pm".

entries.name: fixedDigitsIn
signatures: fixedDigitsIn(fragment: String, width: Integer, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
entries.summary: Reads `fragment` as exactly `width` ASCII digits, as `digitsIn` does. ISO 8601 fields have a fixed width: "14", never "2".

entries.name: digitsToInteger
entries.summary: Reads text of ASCII digits only. Unlike `Integer.parse`, it rejects a sign, which has no place inside an ISO 8601 field.

entries.name: parseFraction
signatures: parseFraction(text: String, whole: String) -> Result<Integer, TimeError>
entries.summary: Reads the digits after a decimal point as nanoseconds: "5" is 500000000. Empty text, or more than nine digits, is an `InvalidFormat` error.

entries.name: splitOffset
entries.summary: Splits text such as "14:03:00+02:00" into the time and the offset. With no offset, the offset part is "Z", for UTC.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: Renders the time structurally, for debugging output.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the time in ISO 8601 form, which is what interpolation and `IO.printLine` show.

entries.name: secondsSinceMidnight
entries.summary: Returns the number of whole seconds from midnight to this time of day.

entries.name: before?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when this time of day is earlier than `other`.

entries.name: after?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when this time of day is later than `other`.

Returns the time of day `span` later, wrapping around midnight.

A `Time` has no date to carry into, so 23:00 plus 2 hours is 01:00. Use `DateTime` to see the day change. Fractions of a second carry into the seconds.
Returns the time of day `span` earlier, wrapping around midnight.

entries.name: addSeconds
entries.summary: Returns the time of day `count` seconds later, wrapping around midnight.

entries.name: addMinutes
entries.summary: Returns the time of day `count` minutes later, wrapping around midnight.

entries.name: addHours
entries.summary: Returns the time of day `count` hours later, wrapping around midnight.

entries.name: until
entries.summary:
Returns the time from this time of day to `other` on the same day.

It is negative when `other` is earlier, and keeps fractions of a second.

entries.name: iso
entries.summary: Returns the time of day as ISO 8601 text, with a fraction of a second only when it is not zero.

entries.name: compareTo
entries.summary: Compares this time of day with `other`, nanoseconds included.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the error as the sentence `Time.errorMessage` gives, so `"${e}"` reads as a message.

entries.name: Truthyable
entries.summary:
Types whose values can be asked whether they count as true.

Only `false` and `None` are falsy. Every other value is truthy, including `0`, `""` and `[]`. `if` and `while` take only a `Bool`, so call `truthy?` or `falsy?` to apply this rule; `Assert.truthy` uses it too.

```kex
0.truthy?       # => true
"".truthy?      # => true
[].truthy?      # => true
None.truthy?    # => false
false.truthy?   # => false
```

To ask whether a value is empty, use `Blankable`'s `blank?` and `present?`.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Returns `true` unless the value is `false` or `None`.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Returns the boolean itself.

entries.name: not
entries.summary:
Returns the negation of this boolean, the same as `!flag`.

It reads better than `!` at the end of a chain.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Always returns `true`, including for zero. Write `count == 0` when zero matters.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Always returns `true`, including for zero.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Always returns `true`, including for the empty string. Use `blank?` to treat an empty or whitespace-only string as nothing.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Just`, even `Just(false)`, and `false` for `None`.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Always returns `true`, including for the empty list. Use `empty?` or `blank?` to test for an empty list.

entries.name: truthy?
entries.summary: Always returns `true`, including for the empty map.

entries.name: Type
entries.summary:
Types as values.

`Type.of(x)` returns the type of a value as a record you can print, compare and take apart:

```kex
Type.of(42)                  # => Type { args: [], name: "Integer", pure?: true }
Type.of([1, 2]).to(String)   # => Just("[Integer]")
Type.of(x) == Type.of(y)     # compares like any record
Type.of(due).fieldNames      # => ["year", "month", "day"]
```

Where it can, the answer comes from the type checker, which knows things a value does not carry, such as the error type of an `Ok` or the element type of an empty list. Where the checker has no concrete type (untyped code, `--no-check`, a value received from another process), the value itself is inspected, and that answer is less complete: an empty list has no element to look at, and a `Result` holds only one side.

entries.name: Type
signatures: parsed(_: Any?, _expected: Type, _text: String) -> Result<Any, String>
entries.summary: Building and obtaining `Type` values.

entries.name: of
entries.summary:
Returns the type of `value`.

The name of a record or sum type, used as a value, stands for the type itself: `Type.of(User)` is `User`'s type. A library can take a `Type<T>` parameter this way and so learn its `T` from the caller.

entries.name: named
entries.summary: Returns the type with this name and no arguments, for comparing with `Type.of`.

entries.name: generic
entries.summary: Returns the type with this name and these type arguments.

entries.name: function
entries.summary: Returns the function type with these parameter types and result type.

entries.name: returnedBy
entries.summary:
Returns the return type of a named function, as the checker sees it.

Only a named function works. Passing a lambda, a function held in a variable or an overloaded name is a compile error.

entries.name: fieldValues
entries.summary:
Returns a record's field values in declaration order, or `None` for anything that is not a record.

The order is that of `Type.of(record).fields`, so the two zip into name/value pairs. This lets generic code such as an encoder read a record without knowing its type. A tuple is not a record; use its `items`.

entries.name: Field
entries.summary: A record field, as `Type.fields` describes it.

entries.name: Constructor
entries.summary: A sum type's constructor, as `Type.constructors` describes it.

entries.name: parsed
signatures: parsed(_: Any?, _expected: Type, _text: String) -> Result<Any, String>
entries.summary: Turns the result of a text conversion into a `Result`, with an error naming `expected` and `text` when the conversion gave `None`.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `text` as a value of this field's declared type, as `Type.parse` does, with the field's name in the error.

Use it to turn text from a database row or a form into the typed values `construct` takes.

entries.name: Type<T>
entries.summary: Reflection functions on runtime type values.

entries.name: fields
entries.summary:
Returns a record type's fields in declaration order, or `[]` for anything that is not a record.

Each field has its name, its declared type and whether it may be left out. The types are as declared: `Integer?` is `Type { name: "Option", args: [Integer] }`, and a type parameter keeps its own name.

entries.name: fieldNames
entries.summary: Returns a record type's field names in declaration order, or `[]` for anything that is not a record.

entries.name: constructors
entries.summary: Returns a sum type's constructors in declaration order, each with its name and argument types, or `[]` for anything that is not a sum type.

entries.name: constructorNames
entries.summary: Returns a sum type's constructor names in declaration order, or `[]` for anything that is not a sum type.

entries.name: constructorValues
entries.summary: Returns the stored spelling of each constructor without arguments, in snake case and declaration order: `ReadOnly` is `"read_only"`.

entries.name: constructorValue
entries.summary: Returns the stored spelling of `value`, a constructor of this type without arguments, or `None` when it is not one.

entries.name: construct
entries.summary:
Builds a record of this type from a map of field names to values.

Use it in a library that maps data it does not define, such as database rows, decoded JSON or form fields, onto the caller's records. A field missing from `values` takes its default, or `None` when it is optional. A missing required field, a key that names no field and a value of the wrong type are each an error naming the field. Values are not converted: `"5"` is not an `Integer`, so convert first, with `Type.Field.parse` or `"5".to(Integer)`.

entries.name: variant
entries.summary:
Builds the value of this sum type's constructor `name` from its arguments, for example turning `"Direct"` read from a database back into `Direct`.

The arguments are checked against the constructor's declared types and number.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `text` as a value of this type, for turning text from a database cell, form field or query parameter into a value for `construct`.

`String`, `Integer`, `Float`, `Bool` (`"true"` or `"false"`) and `Char` (one character) are read as written. `T?` parses a `T` and wraps it in `Just`; no text parses as `None`, so leave an absent value out of `construct`'s map. A constructor without arguments is read from its exact name, its name in any case, or its snake-case spelling: `"channel"` is `Channel` and `"read_only"` is `ReadOnly`. A spelling that matches more than one constructor is an error.

entries.name: nullaryNamed
entries.summary: The nullary constructor `text` names, including its snake-case value. Exact constructor names take precedence; a normalized spelling must be unambiguous.

entries.name: record?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the type is a record with at least one field.

entries.name: adt?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the type is a sum type.

entries.name: to
entries.summary:
Returns the type as it is written in source, always wrapped in `Just`.

A list reads as `[Integer]`, a tuple as `(Integer, String)`, an optional as `String?`, a map as `{String: Integer}`, and a function as its signature.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Returns the type as it is written in source. String interpolation uses this.

entries.name: Unit
entries.summary: The trait every unit implements: its conversion factor to the base unit of its dimension, the dimension, and its symbol.

entries.name: factor
entries.summary: Returns how many base units one of this unit is: `60.0` for a minute, since the base unit of time is the second.

entries.name: kind
entries.summary: Returns the dimension this unit measures, as an atom. Only measures of the same dimension can be added or converted into each other.

entries.name: symbol
entries.summary: Returns the symbol a measure in this unit is shown with.

entries.name: measureKind
entries.summary: Returns the dimension of a measure, as an atom.

entries.name: measureSymbol
entries.summary: Returns the symbol of a measure's unit.

entries.name: measureFactor
entries.summary: Returns the conversion factor of a measure's unit to its base unit.

entries.name: UnitDefinition
entries.summary:
A unit described by its fields instead of a constructor.

Every `Measure` stores its unit this way. Prefixed units and units made by arithmetic, such as `m^2` from squaring a length or a kilo- prefix on a base unit, exist only in this form.

entries.name: factor
entries.summary: How many base units one of this unit is.

entries.name: kind
entries.summary: Which dimension this unit measures.

entries.name: symbol
entries.summary: How the unit is written.

entries.name: Quantity
entries.summary:
The dimensions a measure can have, as types: the `D` of `Measure<D>`.

Each unit fixes its dimension: `1.second` is a `Measure<Quantity.Time>` and `1.meter` a `Measure<Quantity.Length>`, so adding, comparing or ordering measures of different dimensions is a type error. These types have no values. Unit arithmetic gives a dimension too: `1.watt * 1.hour` is a `Measure<Quantity.Energy>`, from the products `Units.SI` declares, and a product it does not declare is a type error.

entries.name: Area
entries.summary: Dimensions derived from others by the products and quotients in `Units.SI`: length over time is speed, speed over time acceleration, force over length pressure, and length squared area.

entries.name: Measure
entries.summary:
A quantity with a unit, of dimension `D`, one of the `Quantity` types.

Every unit module uses this record. `canonical` holds the value in the dimension's base unit and `unit` decides how it is shown, which is how +1.hour + 30.minute+ comes out right and still prints in hours.

entries.name: Duration
entries.summary:
A span of time, which is any measure of time.

`Time`, `Date` and `DateTime` take one: +Date.today() + 3.day+.

entries.name: TimeUnit
entries.summary: The units of time, from nanoseconds to weeks. The base unit is the second.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Time measures from an `Integer`: `5.second`, `90.minute`, `2.week`.

The measure is shown in the unit you named, so `90.minute` prints as minutes, though it holds 5400 seconds as its base value.

entries.name: nanosecond
entries.summary: This many nanoseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: microsecond
entries.summary: This many microseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: millisecond
entries.summary: This many milliseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns this many seconds, as a `Measure`. The second is the base unit of time.

entries.name: minute
entries.summary: This many minutes, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: hour
entries.summary: This many hours, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: day
entries.summary: This many days, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: week
entries.summary: This many weeks, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary: Time measures from a `Float`, for fractional amounts: `1.5.hour`, `0.25.second`.

entries.name: nanosecond
entries.summary: This many nanoseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: microsecond
entries.summary: This many microseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: millisecond
entries.summary: This many milliseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: This many seconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: minute
entries.summary: This many minutes, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: hour
entries.summary: This many hours, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: day
entries.summary: This many days, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: week
entries.summary: This many weeks, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: Measure<D>
signatures: to(String: Type, in: TimeUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary:
Equality and ordering of measures by quantity: `1.minute == 60.second` and `1.kilometer == 1000.meter`, whatever units each was written in.

Measures of different dimensions are never equal, and ordering them, as in `1.second < 1.meter`, is a type error. A measure whose dimension is only known at run time, made by unit arithmetic, is compared by its base-unit value alone.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(String: Type, in: TimeUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary: Renders the measure in its own unit.

entries.name: scaled
entries.summary:
Returns the measure in the largest unit in which its size is at least 1.

Time picks from nanoseconds through weeks, data from bytes through terabytes, and SI dimensions from the decimal prefixes nano through giga. Zero is shown in the base unit, and a value smaller than the smallest unit in that unit. Measures of other dimensions keep their unit.

entries.name: scaled
entries.summary: Returns the measure in the largest unit in which its size is at least 1, as `scaled` does. With `binary` true, data uses KiB through TiB.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the measure as its number and unit symbol, which is what `IO.printLine` and interpolation show. `inspected` and the REPL show the record's fields instead.

entries.name: scale
entries.summary:
Multiplies the measure by a plain number, keeping its unit.

Three times a two-second interval is six seconds, shown in seconds.

entries.name: raisedUnit
entries.summary: Returns this measure's unit raised to `exponent`, for `squared` and `cubed`: the factor raised to that power, a notation such as `m^2`, and the given dimension.

entries.name: convertTo
entries.summary:
Converts the measure to another unit of the same dimension.

Units from opt-in modules such as `Units.SI` and `Units.Data` work too. Converting to a unit of another dimension, such as seconds to meters, is an `Error`.

entries.name: convert
entries.summary: Converts the measure to another time unit; `convertTo` for time units only.

Adds two measures of the same dimension.

The units can differ. The sum is shown in the left operand's unit. Adding measures of different dimensions does not type-check.

Subtracts a measure of the same dimension.

As with +++, the result is shown in the left operand's unit.

entries.name: inOwnUnit
entries.summary: Returns a measure of `total` base units, shown in this measure's unit.

entries.name: scaledValue
entries.summary: Divides a canonical value by a unit factor. The conversion is exact in principle (0.000005 W is 5 μW), but neither number is exactly representable in binary, so the quotient can land an ulp or two off (5.000000000000001). Round back to 15 significant digits, comfortably inside a double's ~15.95, so converted measures read the way they were written.
Returns `true` when `other` is the same quantity of the same dimension.

entries.name: compare
entries.summary: Compares this quantity with `other`, a measure of the same dimension.
The ordering operators of `Comparable`, typed to take only a measure of the same dimension.

entries.name: Measure<Quantity.Length>
entries.summary: Powers of a length that have a dimension: `3.meter ^ 2` is an area and `2.meter ^ 3` a volume, the exponent literal choosing which. Other powers go through `pow` in `Units.Dynamic`, which checks them at run time.
Returns the length squared, the same as `squared`.

entries.name: squared
entries.summary: Returns the length squared, which is an area.

entries.name: cubed
entries.summary: Returns the length cubed, which is a volume and converts to litres.

entries.name: Units
entries.summary:
The time units under the `Units` name. They are also in the prelude.

`Units.Hour` and `Hour` are the same constructor: they match the same patterns and compare equal. The qualified name makes the unit family explicit.

```kex
90.minute.to(String, in: Units.Hour)   # => Just("1.5 h")
```

entries.name: URI
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>

entries.name: URI
entries.summary:
Parses, builds and resolves URIs and URLs, and encodes query strings and HTML forms.

Parsing follows RFC 3986 strictly and keeps the text as it was written: `string` gives back the exact input. Normalizing is a separate step, done by `normalize` and `equivalent?`.

```kex
using URI

let base = URL.parse("https://example.test/a/").try
let reference = URI.parse("../items?limit=10").try
base.resolve(reference).try.string   # => "https://example.test/items?limit=10"
```

A parsed RFC 3986 URI reference: an absolute URI or a relative one.

Make one with `URI.parse` or `URI.fromIRI`, which check the syntax.

entries.name: URL
entries.summary:
An absolute URI with a host, such as an HTTP URL.

Every `URL` has a scheme and a host, so `scheme` and `host` return them directly, where the `URI` versions return optionals. Make one with `URL.parse` or `URL.build`.

entries.name: Host
entries.summary: A URI's host as written, in `display`, and in lowercase ASCII (IDNA) form, in `ascii`.

entries.name: Query
entries.summary:
The entries of a URI query string, in order.

Order and repeated keys are kept, since APIs rely on them: `tag=kex&tag=beam` has two entries. A value of `None` is a bare key, as in `?debug`; `Just("")` is a key with an empty value, as in `?debug=`.

entries.name: Form
entries.summary:
The fields of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, in order.

Forms encode a space as +++. In a `Query`, +++ is a literal plus sign.

entries.name: URIError
entries.summary: The error returned when a URI cannot be parsed, converted or resolved: its `kind`, and a message for a person to read.

entries.name: URIErrorKind
entries.summary: What kind of problem a `URIError` reports.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an RFC 3986 URI reference, which may be relative.

The text must be ASCII, with anything else already percent-encoded; use `URI.fromIRI` for text a person typed. Use `URL.parse` when the input must be a complete URL with a scheme and host.

entries.name: fromIRI
entries.summary:
Converts an internationalized address (an IRI) to an ASCII URI.

The host is converted with IDNA, and the rest of the non-ASCII text is percent-encoded as UTF-8. Use it for addresses people type or paste; `parse` rejects non-ASCII text.

entries.name: URI.URL
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an absolute URL with a scheme and host.

A relative reference is a `NotAbsolute` error, and a URI without a host, such as `mailto:ada@example.com`, is `MissingAuthority`.

entries.name: build
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>
entries.summary:
Builds a URL from a scheme, a host, path segments and a query.

Pass the path segments and query values unencoded. Each segment is encoded on its own, so a `/` inside a value stays part of that segment. The scheme and host are lowercased. The host must be ASCII: an international name has to be given in its `xn--` form.

entries.name: from
entries.summary:
Builds a query from a list of entries, keeping their order, repeated keys and bare keys.

A `None` value is encoded as a bare key, and `Just("")` as a key with an equals sign, so `?debug` and `?debug=` stay different.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses a query string, decoding percent escapes.

A +++ stays a plus sign; use `Form.parse` for form bodies, where it means a space.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Builds a form from a list of fields, keeping their order and repeated names.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Parses an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, where +++ means a space.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the URI exactly as it was parsed.

entries.name: normalize
entries.summary:
Returns the URI in RFC 3986 normal form.

The scheme and host are lowercased, needless percent escapes are decoded, and `.` and `..` path segments are resolved. Parsing never does this by itself, because signatures, cache keys and logs may depend on the exact text.

entries.name: equivalent?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the two URIs are the same after normalizing.

`==` compares the text as written.

entries.name: resolve
entries.summary: Resolves `reference` against this URI, as a browser resolves a link against the page it is on.

entries.name: scheme
entries.summary: Returns the scheme in lowercase, or `None` for a relative reference.

entries.name: host
entries.summary: Returns the host, or `None` when the URI has none.

entries.name: query
entries.summary:
Returns the query, or `None` when the URI has no `?`.

A URI ending in a bare `?` has a query with no entries, which is not the same as `None`.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`, as `showValue` does.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the URL exactly as it was parsed.

entries.name: normalize
entries.summary: Returns the URL in RFC 3986 normal form.

entries.name: equivalent?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the two URLs are the same after normalizing.

entries.name: resolve
entries.summary:
Resolves `reference` against this URL.

The result must still be a URL, so a reference without a host, such as `mailto:ada@example.com`, is a `MissingAuthority` error.

entries.name: scheme
entries.summary: Returns the scheme in lowercase.

entries.name: host
entries.summary: Returns the host.

entries.name: query
entries.summary: Returns the query, or `None` when the URL has no `?`.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the URL with any password in it replaced by `***`.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: Renders the URL with any password in it replaced by `***`, as `showValue` does.

entries.name: encode
entries.summary: Encodes the query by RFC 3986 rules, percent-encoding a +++ in a value.

entries.name: encode
entries.summary: Encodes the form by HTML form rules, which write a space as +++.

signatures: run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X

entries.summary:
Running an operation until it succeeds or a `Schedule` runs out.

`run` calls the block at once. An `Ok` result is returned; an `Error` is retried after a wait, and when the schedule runs out the last error is returned as it is. To choose yourself what to retry, return `again` or `done` from the block.

An HTTP 429 or 503 response is `Ok(response)`, so retrying on a status needs `again`. Only retry a write when repeating it is harmless, for example with an idempotency key. The schedule limits the time spent sleeping, not the time spent in the operation, so give requests their own timeouts.

entries.name: Schedule
entries.summary:
The attempt limit and the waits `run` uses between attempts.

Every field has a default: three attempts, a first wait of 100 ms that doubles each time up to 5 seconds, and 20% jitter. A schedule only holds settings, so each `run` that uses it starts again from the first attempt.

entries.name: Decision
entries.summary:
A block's decision whether to retry, carrying its result.

From `run`, `Done(value)` means the block chose to stop, and `Again(value)` means it still wanted to retry when the schedule ran out. The value can be anything, including an `Error`.

entries.name: again
entries.summary: Returns `Again(value)`, asking `run` to try again if the schedule allows.

entries.name: done
entries.summary: Returns `Done(value)`, telling `run` to stop with `value`, whether that is a success or a failure not worth retrying.

entries.name: Info
entries.summary:
What `run` passes to `onRetry` just before it waits for the next attempt.

`onRetry` is called only when another attempt will follow, never after a success, a `done`, or the last attempt. The durations count sleep only, not time spent in the operation.

entries.name: run
signatures: run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X
entries.summary:
Calls `operation` until it succeeds, returns `done`, or runs out of attempts or sleep time, and returns its last result.

The first call happens at once, and each later one after a wait. Named timing options override that field of `schedule` for this run only.

When the block returns a `Result`, `Ok` stops and `Error` is retried. When it returns `done(value)` or `again(value)`, it decides itself. Use one of the two forms throughout the block. An error raised inside the block is not caught or retried.

Settings out of range are adjusted, not rejected: attempts below 1 become 1, negative durations zero, a backoff below 1 becomes 1, and jitter and the random samples are clamped to 0..1.

`Done(Error(...))` means the block gave up on an error not worth retrying. `Again(Ok(response))` means a response the block rejected, such as a 503, kept coming until the schedule ran out. `run` knows nothing about HTTP: deciding which statuses to retry and honouring `Retry-After` are up to the block.

`sleeper` and `random` are for tests, and replacing one leaves the other real. A sample of 0 picks the shortest jittered wait, 0.5 the unjittered one, and 1 the longest. With zero jitter `random` is not called. lint:allow parameter-count — named options make each setting independent

A first-in-first-out queue.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Queue`.

```kex
using Data.Queue

let q = Queue.from([1, 2, 3])
q.enqueue(4).items    # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
q.peek                # => Just(1)
```

The queue is two lists. `front` holds the elements next in line, and `back` holds the newest ones in reverse. `enqueue` adds to the head of `back`, and `dequeue` takes the head of `front`, reversing `back` into `front` when `front` runs out. Both run in amortized constant time.

`items` gives the elements as a list, front first.

The same elements can be split between `front` and `back` in different ways: `Queue.from([1, 2])` and `Queue.from([1]).enqueue(2)` differ inside. `==` compares `items`, so it calls them equal. Map keys and record patterns compare the fields themselves, so to them the two queues differ.

Updates return a new queue. `enqueue!` and `dequeue!` rebind the variable instead.

entries.summary:
Immutable collections of distinct elements.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Set`, which brings in both kinds of set:

```kex
using Data.Set
```

Membership uses the same structural equality as `==` and map keys, so records and tuples are compared by value. Updates return a new set. The `!` forms (`add!`, `delete!`) rebind the variable they are called on to the new set.

```kex
let tags = Set.from(["kex", "beam", "kex"])
tags.count                     # => 2
tags.contains?("beam")         # => true
tags.add("erlang").items       # => ["beam", "erlang", "kex"]
```

The two kinds differ in how they store their elements:

```kex
Set           kept sorted, so iteration is in ascending order and the
              elements must be +Comparable+.
UnorderedSet  hash-based, so +contains?+ is a map lookup and the elements
              need only support equality. Iteration order is unspecified,
              so don't write a test that depends on it.
```

Use `Set` when you will read the elements back out, and `UnorderedSet` when the set is mostly asked `contains?`.

Two sets are equal when they have the same elements. `items` returns the elements as a list, in no particular order for an `UnorderedSet`.


```kex

```

`push`, `pop` and `peek` take constant time. `items` lists the elements bottom to top, the order they were pushed in:

```kex
let s = Stack.from([1, 2, 3])
```

entries.summary:
Parses Kex source code into a structured AST, at run time.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Kex.AST`.

Use it to write tools that read Kex source, such as linters, formatters, documentation generators and code search. The AST covers modules, function signatures, types and records, traits, make blocks, and the doc comments attached to them; `tey docs` builds the standard library's reference from it.

```kex
using Kex.AST

main do
  match Kex.AST.parseFile("src/main.kex") do
    Ok(program) => IO.printLine("${program.items.count} top-level items")
    Error(e)    => IO.printError(e.message)
  end
end
```

The parsing functions return a `Result`, with a `ParseError` when the source does not parse.

TCP, UDP and Unix-domain sockets, and TLS client connections.

Every socket is owned by a process of its own. Functions that can fail return a `NetError`, and closing a socket twice is harmless. Without a timeout argument, accepting and receiving give up after 30 seconds with a `Timeout` error.

Sockets work on BEAM only. On the tree-walking interpreter every operation returns an `UnsupportedBackend` error unless the capability is replaced with a mock such as `Mock.TCP`.

```kex
using Net
using Net.Socket

let listener = TCP.listen(TCP.Endpoint.loopback(Port.from(0).try)).try
let address = listener.localAddress.try
let client = TCP.connect(address).try
client.sendAll("ping".to(Binary).try).try
listener.close
```
